title: Hopfield model for patterns with internal structure
summary: The spherical version of the Hopfield model for pattern recognition is considered in the static limit. Structures inside the patterns are modeled by Gaussian random variables that reward correlation between pairs of spins in a given pattern. The free energy is derived analytically with the replica method. The overlap distribution obeys a self-consistent equation. Coming from high temperatures, a spin glass phase is entered, in which patterns and correlations appear at lower temperatures. For small enough loading capacity, also a glass phase with patterns and correlations appears.

AI.tldr: Spherical Hopfield model with structured patterns analyzed via replica method reveals spin glass phases with pattern emergence at low temperatures.
AI.motivation: To understand pattern recognition in neural networks with structured patterns where correlations between spins are rewarded, extending the classical Hopfield model to include pattern structure.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of free energy using replica method for spherical Hopfield model with Gaussian random variables modeling pattern structure, solving self-consistent equations for overlap distribution.
AI.result: Identified spin glass phase transition: from high temperatures, entering spin glass phase where patterns and correlations emerge at lower temperatures; for small loading capacity, glass phase with patterns and correlations also appears.
AI.conclusion: The spherical Hopfield model with structured patterns exhibits rich phase behavior with pattern emergence in glassy phases, providing insights into associative memory with correlated patterns.

title: Dreaming improves memorization in a Hopfield model with bounded synaptic strength
summary: The Hopfield model provides a paradigmatic framework for associative memory. Its classical implementation, based on the Hebbian learning rule, suffers from catastrophic forgetting: when one attempts storing too many patterns, the network fails to retrieve any of them. Yet, the Hebbian rule does not take into account that synaptic strength is bounded. Introducing this biologically plausible modification, known as "clipping", eliminates catastrophic forgetting; the model is now able to retrieve the most recently seen memories, eliminating older ones. Yet, its memorization capacity is much reduced with respect to the unclipped case. Here, we investigate the effects of adding a "dreaming" phase on the capacity of a clipped Hopfield model. Following a proposal by Hopfield, Feinstein and Palmer, we assume that during the dreaming phase, the model generates random patterns that are then "unlearned". We show that while clipping still removes catastrophic forgetting, alternating learning and dreaming phases improves the memorization capacity and makes the search for optimal performance more realistic from an evolutionary perspective.

AI.tldr: Dreaming phases improve capacity of clipped Hopfield networks by eliminating catastrophic forgetting while enhancing memory retention through random pattern unlearning.
AI.motivation: Classical Hopfield models with Hebbian learning suffer from catastrophic forgetting when storing too many patterns. While synaptic clipping (bounded strength) eliminates catastrophic forgetting, it severely reduces memory capacity. The paper investigates whether adding a "dreaming" phase can improve capacity in clipped Hopfield networks.
AI.method: The study implements a clipped Hopfield model with bounded synaptic strengths. Following Hopfield, Feinstein and Palmer's proposal, the model alternates between learning phases (storing patterns) and dreaming phases (generating random patterns that are then "unlearned"). This creates a dynamic process where the network selectively forgets irrelevant information while preserving important memories.
AI.result: Clipping successfully eliminates catastrophic forgetting, allowing retrieval of recent memories while forgetting older ones. Adding dreaming phases significantly improves the memorization capacity compared to clipped models without dreaming. The alternating learning/dreaming process makes the search for optimal performance more realistic from an evolutionary perspective.
AI.conclusion: Dreaming phases enhance the performance of clipped Hopfield networks by improving memory capacity while maintaining the benefit of eliminating catastrophic forgetting. This biologically inspired approach provides a more realistic model of memory consolidation and offers evolutionary advantages for memory systems.

title: Self-consistent mean-field quantum approximate optimization
summary: We introduce a self-consistent mean-field quantum optimization algorithm that approximates the ground state of classical Ising Hamiltonians. The algorithm decomposes the problem into independent subproblems and treats the interactions between them in a mean-field manner. These interactions are captured by a common environment, constructed self-consistently through a variational quantum circuit, and which modifies the subproblems to account for mutual influence while maintaining computational independence. Consequently, subproblems can be solved individually, avoiding the computational cost of the full problem. We explore the properties of the generated environment and assess the algorithm's performance through extensive numerical simulations on Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glasses. Furthermore, we apply it experimentally to a weighted maximum clique problem applied to molecular docking. This framework enables the solution of problems that would otherwise exceed the qubit and gate counts of current quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: A self-consistent mean-field quantum optimization algorithm that approximates ground states of classical Ising Hamiltonians by decomposing problems into independent subproblems with mean-field interactions captured through a variational quantum circuit.
AI.motivation: To enable solution of optimization problems that exceed current quantum hardware limitations (qubit and gate counts) by developing a decomposition approach that maintains computational tractability while approximating the full problem solution.
AI.method: Decomposes Ising Hamiltonians into independent subproblems, treats interactions between them in a mean-field manner using a self-consistently constructed common environment via variational quantum circuit, allowing individual subproblem solving.
AI.result: Extensive numerical simulations on Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glasses demonstrate algorithm performance, and experimental application to weighted maximum clique problem for molecular docking shows practical utility.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables solving problems beyond current quantum hardware limitations through mean-field decomposition and self-consistent environment construction, providing a scalable approach to quantum optimization.

title: Formally Verifying Quantum Phase Estimation Circuits with 1,000+ Qubits
comment: The work is accepted for presentation as a full research paper in IEEE-DCAS 2026 and the final version will be available via IEEE Xplore after the conference
summary: We present a scalable formal verification methodology for Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) circuits. Our approach uses a symbolic qubit abstraction based on quantifier-free bit-vector logic, capturing key quantum phenomena, including superposition, rotation, and measurement. The proposed methodology maps quantum circuit functional behaviour from Hilbert space to a bit-vector domain. We develop formal properties aligned with this abstraction to ensure functional correctness of QPE circuits. The method scales efficiently, verifying QPE circuits with up to 6 precision qubits and 1,024 phase qubits using under 3.5~GB of memory.

AI.tldr: Scalable formal verification methodology for Quantum Phase Estimation circuits using symbolic qubit abstraction with quantifier-free bit-vector logic, enabling verification of circuits with up to 6 precision qubits and 1,024 phase qubits.
AI.motivation: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) circuits require formal verification to ensure functional correctness, but existing methods face scalability challenges with large quantum circuits. There's a need for scalable verification techniques that can handle realistic circuit sizes while capturing essential quantum phenomena.
AI.method: Uses symbolic qubit abstraction based on quantifier-free bit-vector logic to capture quantum phenomena (superposition, rotation, measurement). Maps quantum circuit functional behavior from Hilbert space to bit-vector domain. Develops formal properties aligned with this abstraction to verify QPE circuit correctness.
AI.result: Method scales efficiently, verifying QPE circuits with up to 6 precision qubits and 1,024 phase qubits using under 3.5 GB of memory. Demonstrates practical scalability for realistic quantum circuit verification.
AI.conclusion: The proposed formal verification methodology provides a scalable solution for verifying Quantum Phase Estimation circuits, bridging the gap between quantum circuit design and formal verification through efficient symbolic abstraction techniques.

title: Distributed g(2) Retrieval with Atomic Clocks: Eliminating Conventional Sync Protocols
summary: We demonstrate a method to measure coincidences between polarization-entangled photons distributed to distant locations, eliminating traditional synchronization by employing a compact, chip-scale atomic clock for precise timing.

AI.tldr: Method for measuring polarization-entangled photon coincidences at distant locations using chip-scale atomic clocks instead of traditional synchronization
AI.motivation: To enable quantum communication and entanglement distribution over long distances without requiring complex synchronization infrastructure, which is typically a bottleneck in distributed quantum systems
AI.method: Use of compact, chip-scale atomic clocks for precise timing at each distant location, eliminating the need for traditional synchronization methods when measuring coincidences between polarization-entangled photons
AI.result: Demonstrated successful measurement of coincidences between polarization-entangled photons distributed to distant locations using the chip-scale atomic clock approach
AI.conclusion: Chip-scale atomic clocks provide a viable alternative to traditional synchronization methods for distributed quantum measurements, potentially enabling more practical quantum communication networks

title: Efficient training of photonic quantum generative models
summary: The topic of generative learning has gained traction within the field of quantum machine learning, in particular with the advent of train-on-classical, deploy-on-quantum methods. This approach exploits the properties of intermediate-complexity circuits whose training can be simulated classically efficiently, but that generally require quantum hardware for the corresponding sampling problem. Quantum linear optics possess similar properties, which allows us to propose an efficient training procedure for photon-native quantum generative models based on the maximum mean discrepancy, where the deployment of the model corresponds to the task of boson sampling. We provide numerical results, propose datasets, and we also explore how initialization strategies and ansatz choice affect the training.

AI.tldr: Proposes efficient classical training for quantum generative models using photon-native quantum linear optics, with deployment via boson sampling, demonstrating numerical results and exploring initialization strategies.
AI.motivation: Leverage the train-on-classical, deploy-on-quantum paradigm for quantum machine learning by exploiting intermediate-complexity circuits that can be simulated classically for training but require quantum hardware for sampling, specifically targeting quantum linear optics systems.
AI.method: Use quantum linear optics to create photon-native quantum generative models with efficient classical training procedure based on maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), where model deployment corresponds to boson sampling tasks.
AI.result: Provide numerical results demonstrating the approach, propose datasets for evaluation, and explore how different initialization strategies and ansatz choices affect the training performance.
AI.conclusion: Quantum linear optics offers a promising platform for efficient train-on-classical, deploy-on-quantum generative models, with boson sampling serving as the deployment mechanism, though performance depends on initialization and ansatz selection.

title: Quantum algorithm for anisotropic diffusion and convection equations with vector norm scaling
comment: This preprint has not undergone peer review or any post-submission improvements or corrections. The Version of Record of this contribution is published in Quantum Engineering Sciences and Technologies for Industry and Services (QUEST-IS 2025), and is available online at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-13855-2_23
summary: In this work, we tackle the resolution of partial differential equations (PDEs) on digital quantum computers. Two fundamental PDEs are addressed: the anisotropic diffusion equation and the anisotropic convection equation. We present a quantum numerical scheme consisting of three steps: quantum state preparation, evolution with diagonal operators, and measurement of observables of interest. The evolution step relies on a high-order centered finite difference and a product formula approximation, also known as Trotterization. We provide novel vector-norm analysis to bound the different sources of error. We prove that the number of time-steps required in the evolution can be reduced by a factor $Θ(16^n)$ for the diffusion equation, and $Θ(4^n)$ for the convection equation, where $n$ is the number of qubits per dimension, an exponential reduction compared to the previously established operator-norm analysis.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithm for solving anisotropic diffusion and convection PDEs using quantum state preparation, evolution with diagonal operators via Trotterization, and measurement, achieving exponential reduction in time-steps compared to previous operator-norm analysis.
AI.motivation: To develop efficient quantum algorithms for solving partial differential equations (specifically anisotropic diffusion and convection equations) on digital quantum computers, addressing the computational challenges of PDE resolution in quantum computing.
AI.method: Three-step quantum numerical scheme: 1) quantum state preparation, 2) evolution using diagonal operators with high-order centered finite difference and Trotterization (product formula approximation), 3) measurement of observables. Novel vector-norm analysis for error bounding.
AI.result: Exponential reduction in required time-steps: factor Θ(16^n) for diffusion equation and Θ(4^n) for convection equation, where n is number of qubits per dimension, compared to previous operator-norm analysis.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum algorithm with vector-norm analysis provides significantly more efficient PDE resolution on quantum computers, demonstrating exponential improvements in computational requirements for both diffusion and convection equations.

title: Large Language Model-Assisted Superconducting Qubit Experiments
summary: Superconducting circuits have demonstrated significant potential in quantum information processing and quantum sensing. Implementing novel control and measurement sequences for superconducting qubits is often a complex and time-consuming process, requiring extensive expertise in both the underlying physics and the specific hardware and software. In this work, we introduce a framework that leverages a large language model (LLM) to automate qubit control and measurement. Specifically, our framework conducts experiments by generating and invoking schema-less tools on demand via a knowledge base on instrumental usage and experimental procedures. We showcase this framework with two experiments: an autonomous resonator characterization and a direct reproduction of a quantum non-demolition (QND) characterization of a superconducting qubit from literature. This framework enables rapid deployment of standard control-and-measurement protocols and facilitates implementation of novel experimental procedures, offering a more flexible and user-friendly paradigm for controlling complex quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: LLM-based framework automates superconducting qubit control and measurement by generating and invoking tools from a knowledge base, enabling rapid deployment of quantum experiments.
AI.motivation: Implementing control and measurement sequences for superconducting qubits is complex and time-consuming, requiring extensive expertise in physics, hardware, and software. There's a need to automate these processes to make quantum experiments more accessible and efficient.
AI.method: A framework that leverages a large language model (LLM) to automate qubit control and measurement by generating and invoking schema-less tools on demand via a knowledge base containing instrumental usage information and experimental procedures.
AI.result: Demonstrated the framework with two experiments: autonomous resonator characterization and direct reproduction of a quantum non-demolition (QND) characterization of a superconducting qubit from literature. The system successfully automated complex experimental procedures.
AI.conclusion: The LLM-based framework enables rapid deployment of standard control-and-measurement protocols and facilitates implementation of novel experimental procedures, offering a more flexible and user-friendly paradigm for controlling complex quantum hardware.

title: Universal Non-stabilizerness Dynamics Across Quantum Phase Transitions
comment: 5 figures in main text, 8 figures in supplementary
summary: Quantum magic and non-stabilizerness are important quantum resources that characterize computational power beyond classically simulable Clifford operations and are therefore essential for achieving quantum advantage. While non-stabilizerness has so far been investigated only at equilibrium, here we extend its dynamics to time-dependent drivings across quantum phase transitions. In particular, we show that the stabilizer Rényi entropies and the cumulants of the Pauli spectrum exhibit universal power-law scaling with the driving rate in slow processes. Moreover, we show that the logarithmic Pauli spectrum is asymptotically Gaussian, implying a lognormal distribution for the Pauli spectrum values. Our results are explicitly demonstrated by exact results in the transverse-field Ising model and by analytical approximations in long-range Kitaev models.

AI.tldr: Non-stabilizerness dynamics in driven quantum systems show universal power-law scaling with driving rate and lognormal Pauli spectrum distribution.
AI.motivation: To extend the study of non-stabilizerness (quantum magic) from equilibrium to time-dependent driven systems across quantum phase transitions, as this resource is essential for quantum advantage beyond Clifford operations.
AI.method: Analyze stabilizer Rényi entropies and cumulants of Pauli spectrum in slow driving processes across quantum phase transitions, using exact results in transverse-field Ising model and analytical approximations in long-range Kitaev models.
AI.result: Stabilizer Rényi entropies and Pauli spectrum cumulants exhibit universal power-law scaling with driving rate; logarithmic Pauli spectrum is asymptotically Gaussian, implying lognormal distribution for Pauli spectrum values.
AI.conclusion: Non-stabilizerness dynamics in driven quantum systems display universal scaling behavior and statistical properties, extending our understanding of quantum magic resources in non-equilibrium settings.

title: Time delocalization and causality across temporal quantum reference frames
summary: In relational quantum dynamics, evolution emerges via the correlations between some system of interest and a clock system, which plays the role of a temporal reference frame. Their combined state satisfies a Wheeler-de Witt-like constraint equation, and therefore does not evolve, leading to a ``block universe'' picture. Here we investigate the interplay of two aspects, namely temporal localization and causal relations, when comparing emergent dynamics with respect to different choices of clock. We first explore the extent to which two clocks can agree on the temporal localization of events. Then, focussing on the operational notion of causality, we require a clearly defined notion of interventions, i.e. quantum operations, and consider two different approaches to modeling these operations within relational dynamics. The first considers their application via the choice of solutions to the constraint equation, i.e.~the choice of which ``history'' is considered. The second approach incorporates the operations into the constraint equation itself and thereby into its solutions, giving a dynamical picture of the interventions. From the perspective of a single clock, both approaches allow for a notion of operational causality in relational dynamics. However, for multiple clocks, only the second approach gives a consistent picture regarding causal relations, while necessarily manifesting some degree of temporal delocalization between frames. Moreover, this second approach, when considering certain cases of temporal delocalization, naturally describes scenarios with indefinite causal order, a well-known quantum feature of operational causality.

AI.tldr: Relational quantum dynamics studies how evolution emerges from correlations between a system and a clock, constrained by a Wheeler-de Witt-like equation. The paper investigates how different clock choices affect temporal localization and causal relations, comparing two approaches to modeling quantum operations/interventions within this framework.
AI.motivation: To understand the interplay between temporal localization and causal relations when comparing emergent dynamics with respect to different clock choices in relational quantum dynamics, and to establish consistent operational notions of causality across multiple temporal reference frames.
AI.method: Two approaches to modeling quantum operations/interventions: 1) Applying operations via choice of solutions to the constraint equation (choice of "history"), 2) Incorporating operations into the constraint equation itself, making them part of the dynamical picture. The study compares these approaches regarding temporal localization agreement between clocks and consistency of causal relations.
AI.result: From a single clock perspective, both approaches allow operational causality. However, for multiple clocks, only the second approach (incorporating operations into the constraint equation) gives consistent causal relations, though it manifests temporal delocalization between frames. This approach naturally describes scenarios with indefinite causal order when considering certain cases of temporal delocalization.
AI.conclusion: The consistent description of causal relations across multiple clocks in relational quantum dynamics requires incorporating quantum operations into the constraint equation itself, which necessarily involves temporal delocalization between frames and can naturally lead to indefinite causal order scenarios.

title: The Structure of Circle Graph States
summary: Circle graph states are a structurally important family of graph states. The family's entanglement is a priori high enough to allow for universal measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC); however, MBQC on circle graph states is actually efficiently classically simulable. In this work, we paint a detailed picture of the local equivalence of circle graph states. First, we consider the class of all graph states that are local unitary (LU)-equivalent to circle graph states. In graph-theoretical terms, this LU-equivalence class is the set of all graphs reachable from the family of circle graphs by applying $r$-local complementations. We prove that the only graph states that are LU-equivalent to circle graph states are circle graph states themselves: circle graphs are closed under $r$-local complementation. Second, we show that bipartite circle graph states, i.e., 2-colorable circle graph states, are in one-to-one correspondence with planar code states, on which MBQC is known to be efficiently classically simulable. Leveraging this correspondence, we present alternative, simple proofs that (1) if a planar code state is LU-equivalent to a stabilizer state, they are in fact local Clifford (LC)-equivalent to it and that (2) MBQC on all circle graph states is efficiently classically simulable. Third and finally, we demonstrate that the problem of counting the number of graph states LU-equivalent to a given graph state is $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard.

AI.tldr: Circle graph states are closed under local unitary equivalence, bipartite ones correspond to planar code states (classically simulable), and counting LU-equivalent graph states is #P-hard.
AI.motivation: To understand the local equivalence structure of circle graph states, which have high entanglement but surprisingly allow efficient classical simulation of MBQC, and to characterize their relationship with planar code states.
AI.method: 1) Prove circle graphs are closed under r-local complementations (LU-equivalence). 2) Establish one-to-one correspondence between bipartite circle graph states and planar code states. 3) Use this correspondence to provide alternative proofs about LC-equivalence and classical simulability. 4) Prove #P-hardness of counting LU-equivalent graph states.
AI.result: 1) Circle graph states are closed under LU-equivalence (only circle graphs are LU-equivalent to circle graphs). 2) Bipartite circle graph states correspond to planar code states. 3) MBQC on all circle graph states is efficiently classically simulable. 4) Counting LU-equivalent graph states is #P-hard.
AI.conclusion: Circle graph states form a structurally rich family with surprising properties: despite high entanglement, MBQC on them is classically simulable, they're closed under LU-equivalence, and bipartite ones correspond to planar codes, providing insights into the boundary between quantum advantage and classical simulability.

title: Quantum Sensing of Birefringence Beyond the Classical Limit with a Hyper-Entangled SU(1,1) Interferometer
summary: Quantum interferometric sensing plays a crucial role in a wide range of applications, including quantum metrology, quantum imaging, and quantum lithography, where minute phase shifts carry valuable physical information. The strength of quantum sensing lies in surpassing classical sensitivity limits, particularly through the use of quantum entanglement and squeezing to suppress optical shot noise. Birefringence sensing is crucial for various applications, as it provides detailed information about the material's structure, stress, composition, and environmental conditions. We present an interferometric scheme for detecting unknown small birefringence beyond the shot-noise limit of sensitivity that leverages the hyper-entanglement within a pair of polarized nonlinear SU(1,1) interferometers, coupled by the birefringence. Specifically, two pairs of crossed-polarization nonlinear media, both generate and measure two-mode quantum light that is squeezed and polarization-entangled. We present a complete theoretical analysis of the interferometer's sensitivity to small birefringence under realistic conditions of gain and internal loss, illuminating the potential for enhancement of the sensitivity by 3-15dB in practical, real-world experiments (the exact achievable enhancement is governed solely by the loss).

AI.tldr: Quantum interferometric birefringence sensing scheme using hyper-entangled polarized SU(1,1) interferometers to surpass shot-noise limit with 3-15dB sensitivity enhancement.
AI.motivation: Quantum sensing enables surpassing classical sensitivity limits for detecting minute phase shifts. Birefringence sensing provides valuable material information about structure, stress, composition, and environmental conditions, but current methods are limited by shot noise.
AI.method: Interferometric scheme using hyper-entanglement within a pair of polarized nonlinear SU(1,1) interferometers coupled by birefringence. Two pairs of crossed-polarization nonlinear media generate and measure two-mode quantum light that is squeezed and polarization-entangled.
AI.result: Complete theoretical analysis shows potential for 3-15dB sensitivity enhancement beyond shot-noise limit under realistic conditions of gain and internal loss. The exact achievable enhancement is governed solely by the loss.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum interferometric scheme demonstrates practical potential for enhanced birefringence sensing beyond classical limits using hyper-entangled SU(1,1) interferometers, with sensitivity improvements achievable in real-world experiments.

title: Parallel iQCC Enables 200 Qubit Scale Quantum Chemistry on Accelerated Computing Platforms Surpassing Classical Benchmarks in Ruthenium Catalysts
summary: We introduce a parallel, GPU-accelerated implementation of the iterative qubit coupled cluster (iQCC) method that overcomes the exponential growth of the transformed Hamiltonian -- the principal bottleneck for classical emulation of quantum chemistry circuits. By distributing Hamiltonian terms across compute nodes via bit-wise partitioning and offloading Pauli contractions to GPUs, we achieve speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude over the serial CPU approach. Crucially, iQCC confines the variational evolution to a classically simulable operator subspace by selecting entanglers exclusively from the Direct Interaction Space, which guarantees non-vanishing energy gradients at every iteration and thereby naturally avoids the barren-plateau phenomenon that renders highly expressive quantum circuits untrainable. Leveraging these algorithmic and hardware advances, we simulate electronic-structure Hamiltonians for industrially relevant ruthenium catalysts in the 100--124 qubit regime, completing full ground-state calculations on NVIDIA GPUs in the ranges of 1.2 - 45 hrs and surpassing the accuracy of Density Matrix Renormalization Group. These results effectively de-quantize a significant portion of the NISQ roadmap: quantum advantage for chemistry is often assumed to emerge beyond ${\sim}50$ qubits, yet our work demonstrates that this frontier lies significantly further -- potentially past 200 qubits -- reshaping expectations for where genuine quantum advantage may first appear.

AI.tldr: Parallel GPU-accelerated iQCC method overcomes exponential Hamiltonian growth, enabling efficient simulation of 100-124 qubit chemistry problems with speedups >100x over CPU, surpassing DMRG accuracy and pushing quantum advantage frontier beyond 200 qubits.
AI.motivation: Overcome the exponential growth of transformed Hamiltonian in classical emulation of quantum chemistry circuits, which is the principal bottleneck for simulating quantum chemistry on classical hardware.
AI.method: Parallel GPU-accelerated implementation of iterative qubit coupled cluster (iQCC) method with bit-wise partitioning of Hamiltonian terms across compute nodes, GPU offloading of Pauli contractions, and confinement of variational evolution to classically simulable operator subspace using Direct Interaction Space entanglers.
AI.result: Achieved speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude over serial CPU approach, simulated 100-124 qubit ruthenium catalyst Hamiltonians in 1.2-45 hours on NVIDIA GPUs, surpassing Density Matrix Renormalization Group accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Effectively de-quantizes significant portion of NISQ roadmap, demonstrating quantum advantage frontier for chemistry lies significantly beyond ~50 qubits (potentially past 200 qubits), reshaping expectations for where genuine quantum advantage may first appear.

title: The uncloneable bit exists
summary: We establish quantum uncloneable encryption with unconditional security, preventing two non-communicating adversaries from simultaneously decrypting a single ciphertext $-$ even when both are given the key. Our construction achieves security that approaches the ideal limit at a rate that is exponentially small in the security parameter, without employing any assumptions. Our proof invokes quantum information principles in the fully quantum realm, in a novel setting of cryptography. A decoupling step certifies the statistical independence needed for randomness extraction, and monogamy of entanglement, formalised via strong subadditivity, rules out the sender being highly correlated with two non-communicating adversaries at once. Consequently, no coordinated strategy beats random guessing of the encrypted bit, establishing unconditional uncloneability. This reveals the existence of an uncloneable bit in Nature and delineates a fundamental, physically enforced cryptographic primitive unavailable in classical settings.

AI.tldr: Quantum uncloneable encryption achieves unconditional security against two non-communicating adversaries, even with key access, approaching ideal limits exponentially fast without assumptions.
AI.motivation: To establish a fundamentally secure cryptographic primitive that prevents simultaneous decryption by multiple non-communicating adversaries, leveraging quantum principles unavailable in classical cryptography.
AI.method: Uses quantum information principles in fully quantum realm, with decoupling for statistical independence certification and monogamy of entanglement (via strong subadditivity) to prevent sender correlation with two adversaries simultaneously.
AI.result: Achieves unconditional security approaching ideal limits at exponential rate in security parameter, with no coordinated strategy beating random guessing of encrypted bit.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates existence of uncloneable bit in Nature and establishes physically enforced cryptographic primitive fundamentally unavailable in classical settings.

title: Quantum nonlocality: no, yes, how and why
summary: The problem of the existence of nonlocal effects in Quantum Mechanics is discussed. The problem is divided in two: the first ('soft') one is to explain the violation of Bell's inequalities as a statistical magnitude. This can be achieved by a simple model within non-Boolean Locality and Realism. This result shows that quantum non-Locality as a consequence of the statistical violation of Bell's inequalities is inexistent. The second ('hard') problem is to explain the violation as it is calculated from series of detection outcomes. L.Sica has demonstrated that, in order to violate Bell's inequalities, the series recorded at (say) Bob when the setting at station Alice is alfa, can be different from the series that would have been recorded at Bob if that setting had been alfa'instead. Therefore, non-Locality in the series of detection outcomes does exist. It cannot be experimentally verified because of its counterfactual nature, but is observed in computer simulations. An appropriate computer code is based on the simple model mentioned plus a contextual instruction. It explains 'how' (Sica's) non-Locality arises, and solves the hard problem. 'Why' the contextual instruction exists is explained by Hellwig and Kraus' postulate of covariant quantum state collapse. In consequence, (Sica's) non-Locality is not in contradiction with Relativity but, quite the opposite, it is implied by Relativistic covariance.

AI.tldr: The paper distinguishes between 'soft' and 'hard' nonlocality problems in quantum mechanics, showing statistical Bell inequality violations can be explained without nonlocality, while detection series violations require contextual nonlocality consistent with relativity.
AI.motivation: To clarify the nature of nonlocal effects in quantum mechanics by distinguishing between statistical violations of Bell's inequalities (which can be explained without nonlocality) and violations in actual detection series (which require nonlocal explanations).
AI.method: Divides the problem into two parts: 1) 'Soft' problem addressed using non-Boolean Locality and Realism model to explain statistical violations; 2) 'Hard' problem addressed using L. Sica's analysis showing detection series require contextual nonlocality, supported by computer simulations with contextual instructions based on Hellwig-Kraus covariant collapse postulate.
AI.result: Statistical Bell inequality violations don't require quantum nonlocality, but detection series violations do require contextual nonlocality (Sica's nonlocality) that is consistent with relativistic covariance rather than contradictory to it.
AI.conclusion: Quantum nonlocality as typically understood from Bell inequality violations is a misconception; true nonlocality exists only in detection series and is not experimentally verifiable due to counterfactual nature, but is consistent with relativity through covariant collapse mechanisms.

title: Experimental demonstration of optimal measurement for unambiguously discriminating asymmetric qudit states
summary: Identification of nonorthogonal quantum states without error is crucial for various applications in quantum information technology, as well as the foundations of quantum physics. Theoretical studies have proposed measurements that maximize the success probability of unambiguously discriminating quantum states. However, these methods are not always experimentally feasible, which has led most demonstrations to focus on equiprobable symmetric states. Here, we establish a projective measurement scheme that optimally discriminates multiple asymmetric qudit states. We experimentally demonstrate this optimal projective measurement using a photonic orbital angular momentum state, where asymmetric qudit states are encoded in the Laguerre-Gaussian modes of a heralded single-photon state. Our results have broad applications in high-dimensional quantum state-based quantum information processing, including quantum key distribution and quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of optimal projective measurement for unambiguous discrimination of multiple asymmetric qudit states using photonic orbital angular momentum encoding.
AI.motivation: Unambiguous discrimination of nonorthogonal quantum states is crucial for quantum information technology and quantum physics foundations, but existing optimal theoretical methods are often experimentally infeasible, especially for asymmetric states beyond the equiprobable symmetric case.
AI.method: Established a projective measurement scheme for optimal discrimination of multiple asymmetric qudit states, experimentally implemented using photonic orbital angular momentum states with asymmetric qudit states encoded in Laguerre-Gaussian modes of heralded single-photon states.
AI.result: Successfully demonstrated optimal projective measurement for unambiguous discrimination of asymmetric qudit states, achieving maximum success probability for state discrimination in the experimental setup.
AI.conclusion: The established projective measurement scheme and experimental demonstration have broad applications in high-dimensional quantum state-based quantum information processing, including quantum key distribution and quantum sensing.

title: Genuinely entangled subspaces and strongly nonlocal unextendible biseparable bases in four-partite systems
summary: A set of orthogonal pure states is an unextendible biseparable basis (UBB), which means that its complementary subspace contains only genuinely entangled states. UBBs thus serve as an effective tool for constructing genuinely entangled subspaces. If every state within such a subspace exhibits distillable entanglement across all bipartitions, it becomes particularly advantageous for applications in quantum information. In this paper, we mainly conduct research on the 4-qudit quantum systems, where the local dimension $d$ is not less than 3. We present an approach for constructing UBB and prove that the UBB established in this way is strongly nonlocal. We build several genuinely entangled subspaces and demonstrate the distillability of the genuinely entangled subspaces across all bipartitions. In addition, we also describe the specific orthonormal basis for some genuinely entangled subspaces. These results will not only contribute to the development of quantum nonlocality theory, but also provide a crucial theoretical foundation for practical quantum information processing tasks.

AI.tldr: Construction of unextendible biseparable bases (UBBs) and genuinely entangled subspaces in 4-qudit systems (d≥3), proving strong nonlocality and distillable entanglement across all bipartitions.
AI.motivation: UBBs serve as effective tools for constructing genuinely entangled subspaces, which are valuable for quantum information applications when they exhibit distillable entanglement across all bipartitions.
AI.method: Develop an approach for constructing UBBs in 4-qudit quantum systems (local dimension d≥3), prove the constructed UBBs are strongly nonlocal, build genuinely entangled subspaces, and demonstrate distillability across all bipartitions.
AI.result: Successful construction of UBBs with proven strong nonlocality, creation of genuinely entangled subspaces with demonstrated distillable entanglement across all bipartitions, and description of specific orthonormal bases for some subspaces.
AI.conclusion: The results contribute to quantum nonlocality theory development and provide crucial theoretical foundations for practical quantum information processing tasks.

title: Toda-like Hamiltonian as a probe for quantized prey-predator dynamics
summary: Phase-space features of a reduced version of the Toda-like Hamiltonian, $\mathcal{H}(x,\,k)$, written in a form constrained by the condition $\partial^2 \mathcal{H} / \partial x \partial k = 0$, with $x$ and $k$ as canonically conjugate variables, are analyzed in terms of Wigner currents. For Wigner currents convoluted with either thermodynamic or Gaussian ensembles, the underlying Hamiltonian dynamics admits analytic corrections due to quantum distortions over the classical phase-space pattern, computed and interpreted through quantifiers of quantumness and stationarity. Notably, while emulating the Lotka-Volterra (LV) dynamics that describe ecological competition systems, the Toda-like classical dynamics allows for analytical solutions with computable periods corresponding to closed phase-space orbits of isotropic prey-predator population distributions. The essential conditions for understanding how classical and quantum evolution can coexist are provided at different scales of quantumness, driven by the associated convoluting ensemble parameter. In the case of Gaussian statistical ensembles, the exact profile of the quantum distortions over classical prey-predator phase-space trajectories is obtained non-perturbatively. Our results indicate that, besides the classical stability admitted by LV models, the Toda-like patterns also exhibit quantum stability. Therefore, this can be regarded as the first step as a predictive theoretical framework towards more robust descriptions of quantum patterns in competitive microscopic biosystems.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes phase-space features of a reduced Toda-like Hamiltonian using Wigner currents, showing how quantum corrections affect classical Lotka-Volterra ecological dynamics and revealing quantum stability in competitive microscopic biosystems.
AI.motivation: To understand how classical and quantum evolution can coexist in competitive microscopic biosystems, particularly examining quantum distortions over classical phase-space patterns in ecological competition systems described by Lotka-Volterra dynamics.
AI.method: Analyzes phase-space features of a reduced Toda-like Hamiltonian using Wigner currents convoluted with thermodynamic or Gaussian ensembles, with analytic computation of quantum corrections to classical phase-space patterns.
AI.result: Obtained exact non-perturbative profiles of quantum distortions over classical prey-predator phase-space trajectories, showing that Toda-like patterns exhibit quantum stability beyond classical Lotka-Volterra stability, with computable periods for closed phase-space orbits.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a predictive theoretical framework for describing quantum patterns in competitive microscopic biosystems, demonstrating coexistence of classical and quantum evolution at different quantumness scales through ensemble parameter-driven analysis.

title: The helical quantum two-body problem and its wave packet dynamics
summary: We explore the helical quantum two-body problem i.e. two repulsively Coulomb interacting particles confined to move along a helix. The effective potential possesses a tunable number of potential wells superimposed on the repulsive Coulomb interaction that can be varied by changing the ratio of the pitch and radius of the helix. The anharmonicity of these wells depends crucially on this ratio and on the order of the well which can be seen also by analyzing the individual wells energy eigenvalue spacing. Our main focus is the investigation of the quantum dynamics of differently prepared wave packets that scatter from the multi-well potential landscape. We show that there exists a rich pattern forming transient evolution which depends also on the number of bound states of the individual wells. We demonstrate how the multiple wells leave their fingerprints in the dynamics leading, among others, to oscillatory structures on different spatial scales, the formation of beats and pulsed emission from single well localized wave packets due to their intrawell dynamics.

AI.tldr: Quantum dynamics of two repulsively interacting particles on a helix reveals tunable multi-well potentials with rich pattern formation in wave packet scattering.
AI.motivation: To explore the quantum two-body problem on a helical geometry, where the interplay between repulsive Coulomb interaction and helical confinement creates tunable potential wells with interesting dynamical properties.
AI.method: Analyze the effective potential for two repulsively Coulomb-interacting particles confined to move along a helix, varying the pitch-to-radius ratio to control the number and anharmonicity of potential wells, then investigate quantum dynamics of prepared wave packets scattering from this multi-well landscape.
AI.result: The helical geometry creates a tunable number of potential wells superimposed on the repulsive Coulomb interaction. Wave packet dynamics show rich pattern formation including oscillatory structures on different spatial scales, beat formation, and pulsed emission from single-well localized wave packets due to intrawell dynamics, with behavior depending on the number of bound states in individual wells.
AI.conclusion: The helical quantum two-body problem exhibits complex, tunable dynamics due to the interplay between Coulomb repulsion and helical confinement, with potential wells that can be controlled via geometric parameters, leading to rich transient evolution patterns with applications in quantum dynamics and pattern formation.

title: Reconfigurable Superconducting Quantum Circuits Enabled by Micro-Scale Liquid-Metal Interconnects
summary: Modular architectures are a promising route toward scalable superconducting quantum processors, but finite fabrication yield and the lack of high quality temporary interconnects impose fundamental limitations on system size. Here, we demonstrate chip-scale liquid-metal interconnects that show promise for plug-and-play superconducting quantum circuits by enabling non-destructive module replacement while maintaining high microwave performance. Using gallium-based liquid metals, we realize high-quality inter-module signal and ground interconnects, comparable in performance to conventional coplanar waveguide resonators. We illustrate consistent device characteristics across three thermal cycles between room temperature and 15 mK, as well as the ability to reform superconducting connections following module replacement. A width-dependent resonance frequency shift reveals a significant kinetic inductance fraction, which we attribute to the presence of $β$-phase tantalum as confirmed by X-ray characterization. Finally, we investigate power-dependent loss mechanisms and observe high-power dissipative nonlinearities qualitatively consistent with a readout-power heating model. These results establish liquid metals as viable chip-scale interconnects for reconfigurable, modular superconducting quantum systems.

AI.tldr: Liquid-metal interconnects enable plug-and-play modular quantum systems with non-destructive module replacement while maintaining high microwave performance comparable to conventional resonators.
AI.motivation: Fabrication yield limitations and lack of high-quality temporary interconnects impose fundamental constraints on scaling superconducting quantum processors; modular architectures need reconfigurable, non-destructive interconnects.
AI.method: Developed chip-scale liquid-metal interconnects using gallium-based liquid metals to create high-quality signal and ground connections between modules; characterized performance across thermal cycles and module replacements; analyzed kinetic inductance via width-dependent resonance frequency shifts and X-ray characterization; investigated power-dependent loss mechanisms.
AI.result: Demonstrated interconnects with performance comparable to conventional coplanar waveguide resonators; consistent device characteristics across three thermal cycles (room temperature to 15 mK); ability to reform superconducting connections after module replacement; identified significant kinetic inductance fraction attributed to β-phase tantalum; observed high-power dissipative nonlinearities consistent with readout-power heating model.
AI.conclusion: Liquid metals are viable chip-scale interconnects for reconfigurable, modular superconducting quantum systems, enabling plug-and-play operation with non-destructive module replacement while maintaining high microwave performance.

title: Metrology for Quantum Hardware Standardization -- Charting a Pathway: A Strategic Review
summary: Advances in quantum mechanics have long underpinned metrology by enabling practical realizations of units through quantum effects. With the 2019 SI revision, traceability is anchored in defined fundamental constants, reinforcing the quantum-mechanical basis of modern standards. In parallel, quantum technologies are transitioning from laboratory science to engineering and early industrial deployment, bringing familiar pressures for integration, reliability, cost reduction, supply-chain formation, and standardization. The direction of benefit is thus reversing: metrology and precision measurement are becoming enabling infrastructure for the industrialization of quantum technologies. Against this backdrop, this paper surveys the metrology and precision-measurement capabilities required across representative quantum-computing modalities and identifies where electrical and related metrology can contribute to the development, characterization, and reliable operation of quantum hardware. We then discuss cross-cutting measurement needs and standardization opportunities that recur across platforms, and note how similar frameworks can extend to emerging quantum-sensing applications.

AI.tldr: Survey paper examining how metrology and precision measurement are becoming enabling infrastructure for quantum technology industrialization, with focus on quantum computing modalities and electrical metrology contributions.
AI.motivation: Quantum technologies are transitioning from lab science to industrial deployment, creating needs for integration, reliability, cost reduction, and standardization. The relationship between metrology and quantum tech is reversing - metrology is now becoming enabling infrastructure for quantum technology industrialization.
AI.method: Survey approach examining metrology and precision-measurement capabilities required across representative quantum-computing modalities. Identifies where electrical and related metrology can contribute to quantum hardware development, characterization, and reliable operation.
AI.result: Identifies specific measurement needs and standardization opportunities that recur across quantum computing platforms. Establishes framework for how similar metrology approaches can extend to emerging quantum-sensing applications.
AI.conclusion: Metrology is shifting from being a beneficiary of quantum mechanics to becoming critical enabling infrastructure for quantum technology industrialization, with electrical metrology playing key roles in hardware development, characterization, and standardization across quantum computing and sensing platforms.

title: Topological phase transition of deformed ${\mathbb Z}_3$ toric code
summary: We investigate the topological phase transitions of the deformed $\mathbb{Z}_3$ toric code, constructed by applying local deformations to the $\mathbb{Z}_3$ cluster state followed by projective measurements. Using the loop-gas and net configuration framework, we map the wavefunction norm to classical partition functions: the $Q=3$ Potts model for single-parameter deformations and a novel $\mathbb{Z}_3$ generalization of the Ashkin-Teller model (AT$_3$) for the general two-parameter case. The phase diagram, obtained via the projected entangled pair state (PEPS) representation and the variational uniform matrix product state (VUMPS) method, exhibits three phases -- the toric code phase, an $e$-confined phase, and an $e$-condensed phase -- separated by critical lines with central charges $c=4/5$ ($\mathbb{Z}_3$ parafermion conformal field theory) and $c=8/5$, along with isolated antiferromagnetic critical points at $c=1$ ($\mathbb{Z}_4$ parafermion conformal field theory). At these critical points, the system reduces to a square ice model with an emergent $U(1)$ 1-form symmetry, exhibiting Hilbert space fragmentation and quantum many-body scar states. Unlike the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ case, the absence of a sign-change duality leads to a richer phase structure.

AI.tldr: The paper studies topological phase transitions in deformed ℤ₃ toric codes, mapping them to classical statistical models and revealing a richer phase structure than the ℤ₂ case with three distinct phases and multiple critical points.
AI.motivation: To understand topological phase transitions in deformed ℤ₃ toric codes, which differ from the well-studied ℤ₂ case due to the absence of sign-change duality, leading to potentially richer phase structures and novel critical phenomena.
AI.method: Uses loop-gas and net configuration framework to map wavefunction norm to classical partition functions (Q=3 Potts model and novel ℤ₃ Ashkin-Teller generalization). Employs PEPS representation and VUMPS method to obtain phase diagrams.
AI.result: Identifies three phases: toric code phase, e-confined phase, and e-condensed phase. Critical lines have central charges c=4/5 (ℤ₃ parafermion CFT) and c=8/5, with isolated antiferromagnetic critical points at c=1 (ℤ₄ parafermion CFT). At critical points, system reduces to square ice model with emergent U(1) 1-form symmetry, Hilbert space fragmentation, and quantum many-body scar states.
AI.conclusion: The deformed ℤ₃ toric code exhibits a richer phase structure than the ℤ₂ counterpart due to absence of sign-change duality, with multiple distinct phases and critical points described by various parafermion conformal field theories, revealing novel quantum many-body phenomena.

title: Enhancing light-matter coupling for exploring chaos in the quantum Rabi model
summary:
Accessing chaos in the quantum Rabi model (QRM) usually requires operating far from resonance, combined with ultra- or deep-strong light-matter coupling.
  This makes direct experiments challenging.
  In this manuscript, we propose a solution to this challenge by employing an anti-squeezing transformation to the bosonic field.
  Specifically, we demonstrate that this transformation maps a weakly coupled, two-photon driven Jaynes-Cummings model (JCM) to an effective deep-strong-coupling QRM in the squeezed-light frame.
  Using out-of-time-order correlator, Husimi distribution, and linear entanglement entropy, we numerically probe chaos in this coupling-enhanced platform and observe the similar chaotic phenomena as in the ideal QRM.
  We also find the coupling-enhanced model can drive the system deeper into the chaotic regime.
  This establishes coupling-enhanced method as a practical approach to study QRM chaos without requiring intrinsic ultra-strong coupling.

AI.tldr: Anti-squeezing transformation maps weakly coupled two-photon driven JCM to effective deep-strong-coupling QRM, enabling chaotic phenomena study without intrinsic ultra-strong coupling.
AI.motivation: Studying chaos in quantum Rabi model typically requires far-from-resonance operation with ultra-strong or deep-strong light-matter coupling, which presents experimental challenges. The paper aims to overcome this limitation.
AI.method: Employ anti-squeezing transformation to bosonic field, mapping weakly coupled two-photon driven Jaynes-Cummings model to effective deep-strong-coupling QRM in squeezed-light frame. Use out-of-time-order correlator, Husimi distribution, and linear entanglement entropy to numerically probe chaos.
AI.result: Demonstrates similar chaotic phenomena as in ideal QRM, with coupling-enhanced model capable of driving system deeper into chaotic regime. Establishes practical approach to study QRM chaos without requiring intrinsic ultra-strong coupling.
AI.conclusion: Coupling-enhanced method via anti-squeezing transformation provides practical experimental approach to access and study quantum chaos in Rabi model, overcoming previous limitations of requiring ultra-strong intrinsic coupling.

title: Emergence of Classical Dynamics from a Random Matrix Schrödinger Model
summary: The Newtonian motion of a macroscopic particle is derived from the linear Schrödinger equation with a Hamiltonian consisting of the free-particle term and a random Hamiltonian drawn from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. The random term models interaction with the environment. We show that the parameters governing the resulting state-space random walk, together with the treatment of experimentally indistinguishable states as equivalence classes, explain the contrasting behavior of microscopic and macroscopic systems. The analysis extends previous work deriving the Born rule for microscopic particles when the free-particle term is negligible.

AI.tldr: Newtonian motion emerges from Schrödinger equation with random GUE Hamiltonian modeling environmental interactions, explaining micro/macro system differences.
AI.motivation: To derive classical Newtonian motion from quantum mechanics by modeling environmental interactions through random Hamiltonians, explaining why microscopic and macroscopic systems behave differently.
AI.method: Use linear Schrödinger equation with Hamiltonian containing free-particle term plus random term from Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE) to model environmental interactions, analyze resulting state-space random walk, and treat experimentally indistinguishable states as equivalence classes.
AI.result: Derives Newtonian motion for macroscopic particles from quantum mechanics, explains contrasting behavior of microscopic vs. macroscopic systems through parameters of state-space random walk and equivalence class treatment, extends previous Born rule derivation for microscopic particles.
AI.conclusion: Classical Newtonian motion can be derived from quantum mechanics when environmental interactions are modeled via random GUE Hamiltonians, with system behavior differences explained by state-space random walk parameters and equivalence class treatment of indistinguishable states.

title: On the Existence of Algebraic Equiangular Lines
summary: We consider real and complex equiangular lines, generated by unit vectors. We show that, for an arbitrary dimension $d$, if there exists a set of $d^2$ equiangular unit vectors in $\mathbb{C}^d$, then there must exist a set of $d^2$ equiangular unit vectors with all of their coefficients in a number field. This result is motivated by the question of constructing SIC-POVMs in quantum physics and conjectures around them. We discuss applications of our techniques to the case of real equiangular lines and consequences of the above results.

AI.tldr: For any dimension d, if d² equiangular unit vectors exist in ℂᵈ, then there exists such a set with all coefficients in a number field, with applications to SIC-POVMs in quantum physics.
AI.motivation: The research is motivated by questions in quantum physics, specifically the construction of SIC-POVMs (Symmetric Informationally Complete Positive Operator-Valued Measures) and related conjectures about equiangular lines.
AI.method: The paper analyzes equiangular lines generated by unit vectors in real and complex spaces, proving that existence of d² equiangular unit vectors in ℂᵈ implies existence of such a set with coefficients in a number field.
AI.result: For arbitrary dimension d, if there exists a set of d² equiangular unit vectors in ℂᵈ, then there must exist a set of d² equiangular unit vectors with all coefficients in a number field.
AI.conclusion: The results connect geometric properties of equiangular lines with algebraic number theory, providing insights into SIC-POVM constructions and their mathematical foundations, with applications to both complex and real cases.

title: Relaxed parameter sensitivity for multiphoton quantum resonances
summary: Multiphoton resonances demonstrate the physical significance of counter-rotating wave terms in light-matter interactions. These resonances, however, are sensitive to detuning errors, making the phenomena challenging to experimentally observe. In this manuscript, we introduce an optimization strategy to address this problem. By using an optimized parameter segmented sequence (OPSS), the robustness against detuning errors of the high-order quantum state transfers can be substantially improved. We prove the versatility of our strategy against frequency detunings by demonstrating the evolution of two specific models. In both cases, the parameter window for maintaining a high state-transfer fidelity is substantially expanded. We further analyze the output photon flux of the optimized system and, taking the three-photon resonance as an example, demonstrate that the system remains capable of generating a stable output photon flux even in the presence of detuning errors.

AI.tldr: Optimized parameter segmented sequence (OPSS) strategy improves robustness against detuning errors in multiphoton resonances, expanding parameter windows for high-fidelity quantum state transfers and maintaining stable output photon flux.
AI.motivation: Multiphoton resonances demonstrate the significance of counter-rotating wave terms in light-matter interactions but are sensitive to detuning errors, making experimental observation challenging.
AI.method: Introduces an optimization strategy using optimized parameter segmented sequence (OPSS) to improve robustness against detuning errors for high-order quantum state transfers.
AI.result: Parameter window for maintaining high state-transfer fidelity is substantially expanded in two specific models; system remains capable of generating stable output photon flux even with detuning errors (demonstrated for three-photon resonance).
AI.conclusion: OPSS strategy effectively addresses detuning sensitivity in multiphoton resonances, enabling more robust quantum state transfers and stable photon flux generation despite frequency detunings.

title: Critical States Preparation With Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: The fast and efficient preparation of quantum critical states is a challenging yet crucial task for various quantum technologies. This difficulty is most particularly for systems near a quantum phase transition, where the closure of the energy gap fundamentally limits the timescale of adiabatic processes and thus precludes rapid state preparation. We propose a framework using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to rapidly prepare quantum critical states, with broad extendibility to light-matter interaction systems. Specifically, a DRL agent optimizes a set of time-dependent control Hamiltonians to drive the system from an initial noncritical state to a target critical state within a finite time and over experimentally accessible parameter ranges. As a concrete application, we focus on the quantum Rabi model. The DRL-optimized time-dependent control Hamiltonian yield a final state with high-fidelity ($>0.999$) to the target critical state. The protocol can be readily extended to other quantum critical systems described by light-matter interaction models, such as quantum Dicke model. This investigation provides a powerful new framework for preparing and manipulating quantum critical states.

AI.tldr: Deep reinforcement learning optimizes time-dependent control Hamiltonians to rapidly prepare quantum critical states, achieving >0.999 fidelity for quantum Rabi model with extendibility to other light-matter systems.
AI.motivation: Fast preparation of quantum critical states is challenging near quantum phase transitions due to energy gap closure limiting adiabatic timescales, creating a need for non-adiabatic rapid state preparation methods.
AI.method: Deep reinforcement learning framework where a DRL agent optimizes time-dependent control Hamiltonians to drive systems from initial noncritical states to target critical states within finite time over experimentally accessible parameters.
AI.result: Applied to quantum Rabi model, DRL-optimized control yields final state with >0.999 fidelity to target critical state, demonstrating effective rapid preparation.
AI.conclusion: Provides powerful framework for preparing/manipulating quantum critical states with extendibility to other light-matter interaction systems like quantum Dicke model.

title: Analytic formulae for non-local magic in bipartite systems of qutrits and ququints
summary: We conjecture analytic expressions for the non-local magic of bipartite pure qudit states of prime local dimension. Our construction relies on the Schmidt-aligned state attaining the minimum over local unitaries, a hypothesis that we support with numerical evidence for pairs of qutrits and ququints. For composite local dimensions, we find that the analogous expressions do not in general reproduce the global minimum, but can still provide computationally cheap approximations to the non-local magic. We also find that relations between non-local magic and entanglement diagnostics that hold for two qubits generally do not extend to qutrit and higher-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: The paper conjectures analytic expressions for non-local magic in bipartite pure qudit states of prime local dimension, supported by numerical evidence for qutrits and ququints, but finds limitations for composite dimensions and general relationships with entanglement.
AI.motivation: To develop analytic expressions for quantifying non-local magic (a measure of non-stabilizerness) in bipartite pure qudit states, particularly for prime local dimensions, and to understand the relationship between non-local magic and entanglement measures beyond qubit systems.
AI.method: The authors conjecture that the Schmidt-aligned state attains the minimum over local unitaries for non-local magic in prime-dimensional systems. They support this hypothesis with numerical evidence for qutrits (d=3) and ququints (d=5). For composite dimensions, they analyze whether analogous expressions provide accurate approximations to the global minimum.
AI.result: For prime local dimensions, the conjectured analytic expressions appear valid based on numerical evidence. For composite dimensions, the analogous expressions do not generally reproduce the global minimum but can serve as computationally efficient approximations. Additionally, relationships between non-local magic and entanglement diagnostics that hold for two qubits do not extend to qutrit and higher-dimensional systems.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides conjectured analytic expressions for non-local magic in prime-dimensional bipartite systems with supporting evidence, identifies limitations for composite dimensions, and reveals that simple relationships between magic and entanglement observed in qubit systems break down in higher dimensions.

title: Efficient Qubit Simulation of Hybrid Oscillator-Qubit Quantum Computation
summary: We introduce a framework for simulating hybrid oscillator-qubit quantum processors on qubit-only systems through position encoding. By encoding continuous-variable position and momentum wave functions into qubit amplitudes, our method efficiently simulates all Gaussian and conditional Gaussian operations -- encompassing the phase-space instruction set (beam splitter, single-qubit rotation, conditional displacement) and extending to squeezing, conditional squeezing, conditional rotation, and conditional beam splitter -- using $O\!\left(\log^2\!\left(Γ+ \log(1/ε)\right)\right)$ qubit gates per hybrid gate, where $Γ$ is the Fock-level bound and $ε$ is the target precision. This polylogarithmic per-gate complexity represents an exponential improvement over Fock basis encoding approaches, which require exponential quantum or classical resources in the number of qubits per mode. We provide rigorous numerical characterization of quantum Fourier transform errors for Fock-bounded states, enabling precise resource estimation for practical implementations. This work establishes that hybrid oscillator-qubit algorithms can be implemented on qubit processors with polynomial overhead, providing new insights into the computational power trade-offs between discrete-variable and hybrid continuous-discrete-variable quantum computing.

AI.tldr: A framework for simulating hybrid oscillator-qubit quantum processors on qubit-only systems using position encoding achieves polylogarithmic gate complexity, exponentially improving over Fock basis encoding.
AI.motivation: To enable implementation of hybrid oscillator-qubit algorithms on existing qubit-only quantum processors by overcoming the exponential resource requirements of Fock basis encoding approaches.
AI.method: Position encoding of continuous-variable position and momentum wave functions into qubit amplitudes, enabling efficient simulation of Gaussian and conditional Gaussian operations with polylogarithmic gate complexity.
AI.result: Achieves O(log²(Γ + log(1/ε))) qubit gates per hybrid gate (exponential improvement over Fock encoding), with rigorous numerical characterization of quantum Fourier transform errors for practical resource estimation.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid oscillator-qubit algorithms can be implemented on qubit processors with polynomial overhead, revealing computational power trade-offs between discrete-variable and hybrid continuous-discrete-variable quantum computing.

title: Incoherent Operations Enable State Transformations Impossible under Dephasing-covariant Incoherent Operations
summary: We show that incoherent operations (IOs) can achieve the state transformations that are forbidden under dephasing-covariant incoherent operations (DIOs), thereby resolving the open problem posed by Chitambar and Gour [Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 030401 (2016)]. We further demonstrate that no set of IO monotones suffices to characterize state convertibility under strictly incoherent operations (SIOs), and that monotones common to IOs and DIOs are insufficient to characterize convertibility under DIOs.

AI.tldr: IOs can achieve state transformations forbidden under DIOs, resolving an open problem. No IO monotones suffice for SIO convertibility characterization, and common IO/DIO monotones are insufficient for DIO convertibility.
AI.motivation: To resolve the open problem posed by Chitambar and Gour regarding whether incoherent operations (IOs) can achieve state transformations forbidden under dephasing-covariant incoherent operations (DIOs), and to investigate the sufficiency of monotones for characterizing state convertibility under different incoherent operation classes.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of quantum resource theory frameworks, comparing different classes of incoherent operations (IOs, DIOs, SIOs) and their state transformation capabilities. Examination of monotone properties and their limitations for characterizing convertibility under various operation classes.
AI.result: IOs can indeed achieve state transformations that are forbidden under DIOs, resolving the open problem. No set of IO monotones suffices to characterize state convertibility under strictly incoherent operations (SIOs). Monotones common to both IOs and DIOs are insufficient to characterize convertibility under DIOs alone.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchy of incoherent operation classes has distinct state transformation capabilities, with IOs being strictly more powerful than DIOs. The characterization of state convertibility requires operation-specific monotones, and no universal set of monotones exists across different incoherent operation classes.

title: Fictitious Copy Quantum Error Mitigation
summary: Errors are arguably the most pressing challenge impeding practical applications of quantum computers, which has instigated vigorous research on the development of quantum error mitigation (QEM) techniques. Existing QEM methods suppress errors with a varying degree of efficacy but importantly demand significant additional quantum and classical computational resources. In this work, we present Fictitious Copy Quantum Error Mitigation (FCQEM) method which corrects quantum errors without requiring any additional quantum resources and purely relies on using classical postprocessing of a joint probability distribution to correct expectation values. The joint probability distribution can be measured ``fictitiously'' by sampling one copy of noisy quantum circuit twice, or classically squaring probabilities from simply one copy. We show that FCQEM can recover eigenvalues even if exact eigenstates are not prepared. Furthermore, our technique can benefit other noise mitigation techniques with no additional quantum resources, which is demonstrated by combining FCQEM with the Quantum Computed Moments (QCM) method. FCQEM can compensate for noise that is pathological to QCM, and QCM allows for FCQEM to recover the ground state energy with a larger variety of trial states. We show that our technique can find the exact ground state energy of molecular and spin models under simulated noise models as well as experiments on a Rigetti 84-qubit superconducting quantum processor. The reported FCQEM method is general purpose for the current generation of quantum devices and is applicable to any problem that measures eigenvalues of operators on sharply peaked distributions.

AI.tldr: FCQEM is a quantum error mitigation method that corrects errors using only classical postprocessing of joint probability distributions, requiring no additional quantum resources.
AI.motivation: Quantum errors are the main obstacle for practical quantum computing applications. Existing QEM methods require significant additional quantum and classical resources, creating a need for more efficient approaches.
AI.method: FCQEM uses classical postprocessing of joint probability distributions measured "fictitiously" by either sampling one copy of noisy quantum circuit twice or squaring probabilities from one copy. It can be combined with other methods like QCM to compensate for noise pathologies.
AI.result: FCQEM can recover eigenvalues even without exact eigenstate preparation, find exact ground state energies of molecular and spin models under simulated noise, and demonstrate effectiveness on a Rigetti 84-qubit superconducting quantum processor.
AI.conclusion: FCQEM is a general-purpose error mitigation method suitable for current quantum devices that requires no additional quantum resources and is applicable to problems measuring eigenvalues of operators on sharply peaked distributions.

title: Cluster-Adaptive Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization for Strongly Correlated Systems
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures; supplementary information provided as ancillary file
summary: Strongly correlated electronic systems exhibit inherently multiconfigurational wave functions, making it difficult to construct compact variational subspaces that preserve the essential multireference character. Quantum computing has emerged as a promising route to alleviate these limitations, and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) is a representative hybrid approach that uses quantum hardware as a determinant sampler followed by classical diagonalization in the projected subspace. To mitigate hardware noise, SQD employs a self-consistent particle-number recovery guided by a single global reference occupancy vector. However, in strongly correlated, multimodal regimes, this global reference can become mixture-averaged and bias recovery toward a mean pattern, diluting mode-specific occupation structure and degrading the determinant pool. Here, we introduce cluster-adaptive SQD (CSQD), which clusters measurement samples via unsupervised learning and performs particle-number recovery using cluster-specific, self-consistently updated reference occupancy vectors. Under a matched variational budget, we benchmarked CSQD against SQD for N2 dissociation in a (10e,26o) active space and the [2Fe-2S] cluster in a (30e,20o) active space. Our results indicate that CSQD offers an advantage over SQD in estimating the ground-state energy in the strongly correlated regime, lowering the variational estimate by up to 15.95 mHa for stretched N2 and up to 45.53 mHa for [2Fe-2S], with modest additional classical overhead.

AI.tldr: CSQD improves quantum diagonalization for strongly correlated systems by clustering measurement samples and using cluster-specific reference vectors, outperforming SQD in ground-state energy estimation.
AI.motivation: Strongly correlated systems have multiconfigurational wave functions that are difficult to capture with compact variational subspaces. While quantum computing offers promise, existing SQD methods use a single global reference occupancy vector that becomes mixture-averaged in multimodal regimes, biasing recovery and degrading determinant pools.
AI.method: Cluster-adaptive SQD (CSQD) uses unsupervised learning to cluster measurement samples from quantum hardware, then performs particle-number recovery using cluster-specific, self-consistently updated reference occupancy vectors rather than a single global reference.
AI.result: CSQD outperforms SQD in strongly correlated regimes: lowers ground-state energy estimates by up to 15.95 mHa for stretched N2 in (10e,26o) active space and up to 45.53 mHa for [2Fe-2S] cluster in (30e,20o) active space, with modest additional classical overhead.
AI.conclusion: CSQD provides an effective enhancement to quantum diagonalization methods for strongly correlated systems by preserving mode-specific occupation structure through cluster-adaptive reference vectors, improving accuracy in multimodal regimes.

title: Elementary asymptotic approach to the Landau-Zener problem
