summary: We present an asymptotic approach towards the standard Landau-Zener problem based on two linearly independent elementary waves of constant amplitude but time-dependent phase. The two contributions to this phase are quadratic and logarithmic in time and result from the linear chirp of the energies and the lowest order correction in the coupling between the two levels in the long-time limit. Indeed, our solutions subjected to initial conditions at a large but finite time in the past, are valid for large negative and large positive times. Due to their asymptotic nature they are not valid in the neighborhood of the moment when the levels cross. However, as the starting point of the dynamics moves further into the past, the time interval of the break-down of our asymptotic solutions shrinks and vanishes in the limit of the infinite past which corresponds to the standard Landau-Zener situation. Our approach explains not only every feature of the exact solution but yields deeper insights into the origin of the effects. In particular, it (i) brings to light the subtleties involved in the asymptotic limit leading to the standard expressions for the Landau-Zener transition amplitudes, (ii) identifies the logarithmic phase as the origin of the exponential transition probability amplitude, and (iii) reveals the structure of the lowest order corrections to the Landau-Zener result when the starting point is not in the infinite past.

AI.tldr: Asymptotic approach to Landau-Zener problem using elementary waves with time-dependent phase reveals logarithmic phase origin of exponential transition probability and clarifies subtleties in asymptotic limits.
AI.motivation: To develop an asymptotic approach that provides deeper insights into the Landau-Zener problem beyond the exact solution, explaining the origin of exponential transition probabilities and clarifying subtleties in asymptotic limits.
AI.method: Uses two linearly independent elementary waves with constant amplitude but time-dependent phase consisting of quadratic and logarithmic contributions. The phase components result from linear chirp of energies and lowest order coupling correction. Solutions are valid for large negative and positive times but break down near level crossing.
AI.result: The asymptotic approach explains all features of the exact Landau-Zener solution, identifies logarithmic phase as origin of exponential transition probability amplitude, reveals subtleties in asymptotic limits leading to standard expressions, and provides structure of lowest order corrections when starting point is not in infinite past.
AI.conclusion: The asymptotic method offers deeper physical insights into Landau-Zener transitions, clarifying the mathematical origins of key features and providing corrections for finite-time dynamics, while the breakdown near level crossing shrinks as initial time approaches infinite past.

title: Polaron effects on the information backflow in Jaynes-Cummings model
summary: We investigate the influence of phonon degrees of freedom on the qubit dynamics in Jaynes-Cummings (JC) model. A strong qubit-phonon coupling is considered giving rise to Jaynes-Cummings-Holstein (JCH) model. Under anti-adiabatic conditions, we perform a unitary transformation to make the underlying problem tractable through Redfield-type non-Markovian master equation. Analytical expression for the time-dependent coherence is obtained, incorporating both cavity-induced dissipation and phonon-induced dressing effects. The dynamics of JC model is highly non-Markovian for a narrow spectral width and finite detuning. However, a non-zero phonon coupling suppresses these non-Markovian features by effectively reducing the qubit-cavity interaction strength. {It is observed that polaronic dressing effectively supresses the detuning effects. Furthermore, the coherence-based non-Markovianity measure shows an order-of-magnitude suppression in the JCH model, indicating a new dynamical regime, while memory effects extend over a wider range of spectral densities than in the JC model.

AI.tldr: Phonon coupling in Jaynes-Cummings-Holstein model suppresses non-Markovian features by reducing effective qubit-cavity interaction and suppressing detuning effects, creating a new dynamical regime with extended memory effects.
AI.motivation: To investigate how phonon degrees of freedom influence qubit dynamics in the Jaynes-Cummings model, particularly examining the effects of strong qubit-phonon coupling in the Jaynes-Cummings-Holstein model on non-Markovian behavior.
AI.method: Under anti-adiabatic conditions, perform unitary transformation to make the problem tractable, then use Redfield-type non-Markovian master equation to derive analytical expression for time-dependent coherence incorporating cavity dissipation and phonon-induced dressing effects.
AI.result: Phonon coupling suppresses non-Markovian features by effectively reducing qubit-cavity interaction strength, polaronic dressing suppresses detuning effects, coherence-based non-Markovianity measure shows order-of-magnitude suppression in JCH model, and memory effects extend over wider range of spectral densities than in JC model.
AI.conclusion: Phonon degrees of freedom fundamentally alter qubit dynamics by suppressing non-Markovian features and creating a new dynamical regime with extended memory effects, demonstrating that polaronic dressing provides significant control over quantum coherence and non-Markovian behavior in cavity QED systems.

title: Thermodynamic Properties of the Dunkl-Pauli Oscillator in an Aharonov-Bohm Flux
summary: We investigate the thermodynamic properties of a spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ particle described by the Dunkl-deformed Pauli equation in two dimensions in the presence of an Aharonov--Bohm (AB) flux. By replacing the standard momentum operators with Dunkl operators, the Hamiltonian incorporates reflection symmetry together with topological gauge effects. The magnetic flux imposes symmetry constraints on the Dunkl parameters, $ν_1 + \varepsilon ν_2 = 0$, linking the reflection sectors ($\varepsilon = \pm 1$) to the structure of the energy spectrum. Using the exact spectrum, we construct the canonical partition function and derive the thermodynamic quantities including the internal energy, entropy, and heat capacity. The results show that the interplay between Dunkl reflection symmetry and the AB phase leads to distinctive thermal behavior. In particular, the heat capacity exhibits a Schottky-type anomaly controlled by the magnetic flux, while at high temperatures the system approaches the classical oscillator limit.

AI.tldr: Study of thermodynamic properties of a spin-1/2 particle described by Dunkl-deformed Pauli equation in 2D with Aharonov-Bohm flux, showing distinctive thermal behavior due to interplay between reflection symmetry and topological gauge effects.
AI.motivation: To investigate how the combination of Dunkl deformation (incorporating reflection symmetry) and topological Aharonov-Bohm flux affects thermodynamic properties of quantum systems, particularly exploring the interplay between reflection symmetry and gauge effects.
AI.method: Replace standard momentum operators with Dunkl operators in the Pauli equation to incorporate reflection symmetry, include Aharonov-Bohm flux, derive exact energy spectrum, construct canonical partition function, and compute thermodynamic quantities (internal energy, entropy, heat capacity).
AI.result: Magnetic flux imposes symmetry constraints on Dunkl parameters (ν₁ + εν₂ = 0), heat capacity exhibits Schottky-type anomaly controlled by magnetic flux, system approaches classical oscillator limit at high temperatures, distinctive thermal behavior emerges from interplay between Dunkl reflection symmetry and AB phase.
AI.conclusion: The combination of Dunkl deformation and Aharonov-Bohm flux creates unique thermodynamic signatures, with the magnetic flux controlling Schottky anomalies and the system recovering classical behavior at high temperatures, demonstrating significant interplay between reflection symmetry and topological gauge effects.

title: Verified delegated quantum computation requires techniques beyond cut-and-choose
summary: Delegated quantum computation enables a client with limited quantum capabilities to outsource computations to a more powerful quantum server while preserving correctness and privacy. Verification is crucial in this setting to ensure that the untrusted quantum server performs the computation honestly and returns correct results. A common verification method is the quantum cut-and-choose technique. Inspired by classical verification methods for two-party computation, the client uses the majority of the delegated rounds to test the server's honesty, while keeping the remaining ones for the actual computation. Combining this technique with other methods, such as quantum error correction, could help achieve negligible cheating probabilities for the server; however, such methods can impose significant overheads making implementations unfeasible for the near-term future. In this work, we investigate whether cut-and-choose can yield efficient and secure verifiable quantum computation without additional costly techniques. We find that verifiable delegated quantum computation protocols relying solely on cut-and-choose techniques cannot be secure and efficient at the same time.

AI.tldr: Cut-and-choose techniques alone cannot achieve both security and efficiency in verifiable delegated quantum computation.
AI.motivation: Delegated quantum computation requires verification to ensure correctness and privacy against untrusted servers. While cut-and-choose techniques are commonly used, combining them with other methods like quantum error correction imposes significant overheads, making near-term implementations unfeasible.
AI.method: The paper investigates whether cut-and-choose techniques alone can yield efficient and secure verifiable quantum computation without additional costly methods. It analyzes the fundamental limitations of verifiable delegated quantum computation protocols relying solely on cut-and-choose.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that verifiable delegated quantum computation protocols relying solely on cut-and-choose techniques cannot be simultaneously secure and efficient.
AI.conclusion: Cut-and-choose techniques alone are insufficient for achieving both security and efficiency in verifiable delegated quantum computation, indicating the need for alternative approaches or hybrid methods.

title: Chip-Integrated Broadband Multi-Photon Source for Wavelength-Multiplexed Quantum Networks
summary: Quantum networks based on wavelength-multiplexed entanglement enable parallel distribution of quantum correlations, increasing channel capacity for secure communication and distributed quantum information processing. However, broadband integrated sources capable of generating multipartite entanglement beyond photon pairs remain scarce. Here we report on-chip generation of telecom-band four-photon entanglement in a periodically poled thin-film lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguide. Type-0 spontaneous parametric down-conversion provides a phase-matching bandwidth exceeding 200 nm, enabling spectrally separable generation of multi-photon entanglement across the telecom band. The generated photons are encoded in time bins for robust fiber compatibility, and a coherent interface enabling reversible conversion between time-bin and polarization degrees of freedom allows complete quantum state tomography. We measure two-photon entanglement with a brightness of 6.7 MHz/mW/nm and a fidelity of $0.874 \pm 0.002$. At a pump power of 0.08 mW, the four-photon state exhibits a fourfold coincidence rate of 1 Hz and a fidelity of $0.74 \pm 0.01$, representing a threefold improvement over previous integrated platforms. Our results establish LNOI as a scalable platform for broadband multi-photon entanglement and provide a practical route toward dense wavelength-multiplexed quantum networks.

AI.tldr: On-chip generation of telecom-band four-photon entanglement using thin-film lithium niobate waveguide with 200+ nm bandwidth, achieving 1 Hz fourfold coincidence rate and 0.74 fidelity.
AI.motivation: Quantum networks need wavelength-multiplexed entanglement for parallel distribution, but broadband integrated sources for multipartite entanglement beyond photon pairs are scarce.
AI.method: Used periodically poled thin-film lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguide with type-0 spontaneous parametric down-conversion providing >200 nm phase-matching bandwidth. Photons encoded in time bins for fiber compatibility, with coherent interface for reversible conversion between time-bin and polarization degrees of freedom for complete quantum state tomography.
AI.result: Two-photon entanglement: brightness of 6.7 MHz/mW/nm, fidelity of 0.874 ± 0.002. Four-photon entanglement at 0.08 mW pump: fourfold coincidence rate of 1 Hz, fidelity of 0.74 ± 0.01, representing threefold improvement over previous integrated platforms.
AI.conclusion: LNOI established as scalable platform for broadband multi-photon entanglement, providing practical route toward dense wavelength-multiplexed quantum networks.

title: Multi-tasking through quantum annealing
summary: Quantum annealing approximately solves combinatorial optimization problems by leveraging the principles of adiabatic quantum systems. In this approach, the system's Hamiltonian evolves from an initial general state to a problem-specific state. This study introduces multi-tasking quantum annealing (MTQA), a method that enables the parallel processing of multiple optimization problems by embedding them into spatially distinct regions on quantum hardware. MTQA is evaluated using two NP-hard problems: the minimum vertex cover problem (MVCP) and the graph partitioning problem (GPP). This parallel approach optimizes quantum resource utilization by concurrently utilizing idle qubits. The findings demonstrate that MTQA achieves a solution quality comparable to single-problem quantum annealing and classical simulated annealing (SA), while notably reducing the time-to-solution (TTS) metrics. Eigenspectrum analysis further theoretically supports the hypothesis that parallel embedding preserves quantum coherence and does not increase computational complexity by efficiently utilizing available quantum hardware (e.g., qubits and couplers). MTQA enables efficient multitasking in quantum annealing, optimizing hardware utilization and improving throughput for concurrent tasks and demonstrating performance for problems up to 100 nodes in real-world applications.

AI.tldr: MTQA enables parallel processing of multiple optimization problems on quantum annealing hardware by embedding them into spatially distinct regions, achieving comparable solution quality to single-problem approaches while reducing time-to-solution.
AI.motivation: To improve quantum hardware utilization by enabling parallel processing of multiple optimization problems concurrently, addressing the underutilization of qubits and couplers in quantum annealing systems.
AI.method: Multi-tasking quantum annealing (MTQA) embeds multiple NP-hard optimization problems (minimum vertex cover and graph partitioning) into spatially distinct regions of quantum hardware, allowing parallel processing while preserving quantum coherence.
AI.result: MTQA achieves solution quality comparable to single-problem quantum annealing and classical simulated annealing, while significantly reducing time-to-solution metrics. Eigenspectrum analysis confirms preserved quantum coherence without increased computational complexity.
AI.conclusion: MTQA enables efficient multitasking in quantum annealing, optimizing hardware utilization and improving throughput for concurrent tasks, demonstrating practical performance for problems up to 100 nodes in real-world applications.

title: Enhanced security in Quantum Token protocols using Hybrid Spin-Photon Interfaces
summary: Quantum token protocols enable unforgeable quantum tokens promising unconditional security beyond classical cryptographic assumptions. We show here that the three stages of the Quantum token protocols involving the preparation, storage and verification can be made more secure when involving spin-photon interfaces that leverage high fidelity hybrid tripartite (spin-photon-spin) entanglement, Bell state measurements and highly coherent spin quantum memories. Further we describe the physical implementation of various stages of the protocol using the hybrid electron and nuclear spins in diamond interfaced with time-bin photons.

AI.tldr: Quantum token protocols achieve enhanced security through spin-photon interfaces using hybrid tripartite entanglement, Bell state measurements, and coherent spin memories, with diamond-based electron/nuclear spin implementations.
AI.motivation: To improve security in quantum token protocols (preparation, storage, verification) beyond classical cryptographic assumptions by leveraging advanced quantum technologies.
AI.method: Utilize spin-photon interfaces with high-fidelity hybrid tripartite (spin-photon-spin) entanglement, Bell state measurements, and highly coherent spin quantum memories. Physical implementation employs hybrid electron and nuclear spins in diamond interfaced with time-bin photons.
AI.result: Demonstrated that quantum token protocols can be made more secure across all three stages (preparation, storage, verification) using the proposed quantum technologies.
AI.conclusion: Spin-photon interfaces with hybrid tripartite entanglement and diamond-based spin systems provide a practical pathway to enhance security in quantum token protocols beyond classical limitations.

title: Quantum optical impurity models in interacting waveguide QED
summary: We consider a generic model for interacting waveguide QED systems, where photons in a coupled-cavity array localize around atomic impurities while simultaneously interacting through local Kerr nonlinearities. This scenario appears naturally in nanophotonic crystals, circuit QED lattices, and ultracold atomic systems and is governed by the competition between attractive Jaynes-Cummings-mediated binding and intrinsic photon-photon repulsion. We analyze how this interplay affects the formation of localized few-photon bound states and determine the resulting many-body ground states for large periodic arrays of impurities and different filling factors. With the help of large-scale numerical simulations and approximate analytical models, we identify a rich phase diagram featuring Mott-like insulating states as well as superfluid phases with long-range correlations, which are mediated by an unbound, but strongly interacting photonic fluid.

AI.tldr: Study of interacting waveguide QED systems showing competition between photon-atom binding and photon-photon repulsion leads to rich phase diagram with Mott-like insulating states and superfluid phases.
AI.motivation: Understanding the many-body physics in waveguide QED systems where photons localize around atomic impurities while interacting through Kerr nonlinearities, which occurs naturally in nanophotonic crystals, circuit QED lattices, and ultracold atomic systems.
AI.method: Analysis of localized few-photon bound states and many-body ground states using large-scale numerical simulations and approximate analytical models for large periodic arrays of impurities with different filling factors.
AI.result: Identification of a rich phase diagram featuring Mott-like insulating states and superfluid phases with long-range correlations mediated by strongly interacting but unbound photonic fluid.
AI.conclusion: The competition between attractive Jaynes-Cummings-mediated binding and intrinsic photon-photon repulsion in waveguide QED systems leads to diverse quantum phases, including insulating and superfluid states, with implications for quantum simulation and quantum information processing.

title: An elementary proof of symmetrization postulate in quantum mechanics for a system of particles
summary: According to symmetrization postulate for a system of identical particles, wave function has to be completely symmetric or completely anti-symmetric. In this paper we want to mathematically justify this postulate ignoring the spin part of wave function in three dimension. For a system of N identical particles, if the solution to the governing Schrodinger equation meets these criteria: a) the probability density remains invariant when any two particle positions are exchanged over time, b) the wave function is continuous and has a continuous gradient, and the system exhibits the following characteristics: c) the configuration space, which is 3N dimensional, is connected, and d) the potential term in the Hamiltonian is invariant under the exchange of any two particle positions, then the wave function must be either totally symmetric or totally antisymmetric over time.

AI.tldr: Mathematical proof that under specific conditions (invariant probability density, smooth wave function, connected configuration space, symmetric potential), the wave function of N identical particles must be either completely symmetric or completely antisymmetric.
AI.motivation: To provide rigorous mathematical justification for the symmetrization postulate in quantum mechanics, which states that wave functions of identical particles must be either symmetric (bosons) or antisymmetric (fermions), ignoring spin degrees of freedom in three dimensions.
AI.method: Theoretical mathematical analysis based on the Schrödinger equation with specific conditions: (a) probability density invariance under particle exchange, (b) wave function continuity with continuous gradient, (c) connected 3N-dimensional configuration space, and (d) potential term invariance under particle exchange.
AI.result: Under the specified conditions, the wave function must be either totally symmetric or totally antisymmetric over time, providing mathematical justification for the symmetrization postulate without relying on experimental evidence or spin considerations.
AI.conclusion: The symmetrization postulate can be mathematically derived from fundamental quantum mechanical principles under reasonable physical conditions, establishing that identical particles in three dimensions must obey either Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics.

title: High-resolution resonant inelastic X-ray scattering study of W-L3 edge in WSi2
summary: With the advancement of synchrotron radiation and free-electron laser, X-ray quantum optics has emerged as a novel frontier for exploring light-matter interactions at high photon energies. A significant challenge in this field is achieving well-defined two-level systems through atomic inner-shell transitions, which are often hindered by broad natural linewidths and local electronic structure effects. This study aims to explore the potential of tungsten disilicide (WSi2) as a two-level system for X-ray quantum optics applications. Utilizing high-resolution resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) near the W-L3 edge, in this work, the white line of bulk WSi2 is experimentally distinguished, overcoming the spectral broadening caused by short core-hole lifetime. The measurements are conducted by using a von Hamos spectrometer at the GALAXIES beamline of the SOLEIL synchrotron. The results reveal a single resonant emission feature with a fixed energy transfer, confirming the presence of a discrete 2p-5d transition characteristic of a two-level system. Additional high-resolution XAS spectra, obtained via high energy resolution fluorescence detection method and reconstructed from off-resonant emission (free from self-absorption effect for bulk WSi2 sample) method, further support the identification of a sharp white line. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using WSi2 as a model system in X-ray cavity quantum optics and establish RIXS as a powerful technique to resolve fine inner-shell structures.

AI.tldr: WSi2 shows potential as a two-level system for X-ray quantum optics, with RIXS resolving discrete inner-shell transitions despite spectral broadening challenges.
AI.motivation: X-ray quantum optics requires well-defined two-level systems using atomic inner-shell transitions, but these are hindered by broad natural linewidths and local electronic structure effects. The study aims to explore tungsten disilicide (WSi2) as a potential two-level system for this application.
AI.method: Used high-resolution resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) near the W-L3 edge with a von Hamos spectrometer at the GALAXIES beamline of SOLEIL synchrotron. Also employed high-resolution XAS spectra via high energy resolution fluorescence detection and reconstructed from off-resonant emission methods to avoid self-absorption effects.
AI.result: Successfully distinguished the white line of bulk WSi2, overcoming spectral broadening from short core-hole lifetime. Revealed a single resonant emission feature with fixed energy transfer, confirming discrete 2p-5d transition characteristic of a two-level system. Additional XAS spectra supported identification of a sharp white line.
AI.conclusion: WSi2 demonstrates feasibility as a model system for X-ray cavity quantum optics, and RIXS proves to be a powerful technique for resolving fine inner-shell structures despite challenges posed by short core-hole lifetimes.

title: Variational Quantum Dimension Reduction for Recurrent Quantum Models
summary: Recurrent quantum models (RQMs) realize sequential quantum processes through repeated application of a unitary operation on a memory system coupled with a series of output registers. However, such models often rely on unnecessarily large memory spaces, introducing redundancy and limiting scalability. Here, we introduce a \textit{variational quantum dimension reduction} framework that identifies and removes irrelevant memory degrees of freedom while preserving the recurrent dynamics of the target model. Our approach employs two parameterized quantum circuits: a decoupling unitary $V(θ_1)$ that isolates the essential memory subspace; and a compressed recurrent unitary $\tilde{U}(θ_2)$ that reconstructs the dynamics in the reduced space. The optimization is guided by a unified cost function combining decoupling fidelity and dynamical accuracy, evaluated using the \textit{Quantum Fidelity Divergence Rate} (QFDR), a metric that quantifies long-term fidelity per time step. Applied to a cyclic random walk model, our framework achieves up to three orders of magnitude smaller QFDR compared to variational matrix product state truncation, while requiring only trajectory samples rather than explicit state reconstructions. This establishes a scalable, data-driven paradigm for learning minimal recurrent quantum architectures, enabling variational circuit optimization and quantum process compression for near-term quantum devices.

AI.tldr: Variational quantum dimension reduction framework compresses recurrent quantum models by identifying and removing irrelevant memory degrees of freedom while preserving dynamics, achieving superior compression compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Recurrent quantum models often use unnecessarily large memory spaces, introducing redundancy and limiting scalability for near-term quantum devices. There's a need to identify and remove irrelevant memory degrees of freedom while preserving the essential recurrent dynamics.
AI.method: A variational quantum dimension reduction framework using two parameterized quantum circuits: a decoupling unitary V(θ₁) that isolates the essential memory subspace, and a compressed recurrent unitary Ũ(θ₂) that reconstructs dynamics in the reduced space. Optimization uses a unified cost function combining decoupling fidelity and dynamical accuracy, evaluated using Quantum Fidelity Divergence Rate (QFDR) metric.
AI.result: Applied to a cyclic random walk model, the framework achieves up to three orders of magnitude smaller QFDR compared to variational matrix product state truncation, while requiring only trajectory samples rather than explicit state reconstructions.
AI.conclusion: The approach establishes a scalable, data-driven paradigm for learning minimal recurrent quantum architectures, enabling variational circuit optimization and quantum process compression for near-term quantum devices.

title: ZX-Flow: A Flexible Criterion for Deterministic Computation with ZX-Diagrams
summary: Flow criteria are used to efficiently extract computations, either in the form of measurement patterns or quantum circuits, from ZX-diagrams. Existing criteria such as causal flow, generalised flow, and Pauli flow, were all originally formulated for graph states, so they require ZX-diagrams to be in a very particular graph-state-like form. This form is easily broken by applying basic ZX rules and makes establishing some desirable properties very complicated. Here, we introduce a new "ZX-native" flow criterion called ZX-flow, formulated using a new type of decoration of a ZX-diagram we call Pauli semiwebs. These are a generalisation of Pauli webs, which have recently been used extensively in reasoning about fault-tolerant computations in the ZX-calculus. We show that ZX-flow is straightforwardly preserved by all Clifford rewrites and furthermore that a ZX-diagram has ZX-flow if and only if it is Clifford-equivalent to a graph-like ZX-diagram with Pauli flow. Finally, we show that any diagram with ZX-flow can be readily interpreted either as a deterministic measurement-based computation or as a Clifford isometry followed by a sequence of Pauli exponentials. The latter can then be efficiently extracted to a quantum circuit.

AI.tldr: Introduces ZX-flow, a new flow criterion for ZX-diagrams that is preserved by Clifford rewrites and enables efficient extraction of quantum computations, overcoming limitations of previous graph-state-based flow criteria.
AI.motivation: Existing flow criteria (causal flow, generalised flow, Pauli flow) are formulated for graph states, requiring ZX-diagrams to be in restrictive graph-state-like forms that are easily broken by basic ZX rules, complicating property establishment and limiting applicability.
AI.method: Introduces ZX-flow using Pauli semiwebs, a generalization of Pauli webs, which are decorations of ZX-diagrams. Shows ZX-flow is preserved by all Clifford rewrites and establishes equivalence with Clifford-equivalent graph-like diagrams having Pauli flow.
AI.result: ZX-flow is straightforwardly preserved by Clifford rewrites; a ZX-diagram has ZX-flow iff it is Clifford-equivalent to a graph-like ZX-diagram with Pauli flow; diagrams with ZX-flow can be interpreted as deterministic measurement-based computations or Clifford isometries followed by Pauli exponentials.
AI.conclusion: ZX-flow provides a "ZX-native" flow criterion that overcomes limitations of previous graph-state-based approaches, enabling efficient extraction of quantum computations from ZX-diagrams while being robust under Clifford rewrites.

title: System-bath model for quantum chemistry
summary: We propose an approximate mapping of a molecular Hamiltonian to a Hamiltonian of qubits, which allows for high accuracy quantum chemistry calculations of vertical excitation energies of some molecules. The mapping is based on separating of a very small active space of only two orbitals and on modeling the electronic excitations in the remaining orbitals by a set of qubits or, equivalently, by a set of oscillators. This approach is inspired by the Random Phase Approximation (RPA), in which the excitations of electron gas are described by bosonic degrees of freedom. As a result, the Hamiltonian of the molecule is reduced to that of a system-bath model. The "system" part of the Hamiltonian describes the two molecular orbitals -- the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) -- which are populated by two electrons. Two qubits are sufficient to encode the Hamiltonian of such a system. The "bath" consists of oscillators or, equivalently, of two level systems with each of them corresponding to an electron excitation from a doubly occupied orbital below the Fermi level to an empty orbital above the Fermi level. We hope that this mapping can inspire new approaches and algorithms aimed at calculating excitation energies of molecules on near term quantum computers.

AI.tldr: A novel mapping of molecular Hamiltonians to qubit Hamiltonians for quantum chemistry calculations, separating a small active space (HOMO-LUMO) from bath excitations modeled as qubits/oscillators, inspired by RPA for near-term quantum computers.
AI.motivation: To enable accurate quantum chemistry calculations of vertical excitation energies on near-term quantum computers by developing a more efficient mapping of molecular Hamiltonians to qubit Hamiltonians that reduces complexity while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: Separates molecular Hamiltonian into a small active space (2 orbitals: HOMO and LUMO) modeled by 2 qubits, with remaining electronic excitations treated as a bath of oscillators/qubits representing excitations from occupied to unoccupied orbitals, inspired by Random Phase Approximation (RPA).
AI.result: The mapping reduces molecular Hamiltonian to a system-bath model where system part (HOMO-LUMO with 2 electrons) requires only 2 qubits, while bath consists of qubits/oscillators representing electron-hole excitations, enabling potentially efficient quantum computation of excitation energies.
AI.conclusion: This approximate mapping provides a promising approach for calculating molecular excitation energies on near-term quantum computers by significantly reducing qubit requirements while maintaining physical accuracy through system-bath separation inspired by RPA.

authors: A. M. A. S. D. Alagiyawanna
title: Evolution of Photonic Quantum Machine Learning under Noise
comment: 26 pages, 9 figures. Review article. Currently under review at Quantum Machine Intelligence (Springer Nature)
summary: Photonic Quantum Machine Learning (PQML) is an emerging approach that integrates photonic quantum computing technologies with machine learning techniques to enable scalable and energy-efficient quantum information processing. Photonic systems offer advantages such as room-temperature operation, high-speed signal processing, and the ability to represent information in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces. However, noise remains a major challenge affecting the performance, reliability, and scalability of PQML implementations. This review provides a systematic analysis of noise sources in photonic quantum machine learning systems. We discuss photonic quantum computing architectures and examine key quantum machine learning algorithms implemented on photonic platforms, including Variational Quantum Circuits, Quantum Neural Networks, and Quantum Support Vector Machines. The paper categorizes major noise mechanisms and analyzes their impact on learning performance, training stability, and convergence behavior. Furthermore, we review both traditional and advanced noise characterization techniques and survey recent strategies for noise mitigation in photonic quantum systems. Finally, we highlight recent experimental advances and discuss future research directions for developing robust and scalable PQML systems under realistic noise conditions.

AI.tldr: A review paper analyzing noise sources in photonic quantum machine learning systems, covering architectures, algorithms, noise characterization, mitigation strategies, and future directions.
AI.motivation: Photonic Quantum Machine Learning (PQML) offers advantages like room-temperature operation and high-speed processing, but noise remains a major challenge affecting performance, reliability, and scalability. A systematic analysis of noise sources is needed to advance robust PQML implementations.
AI.method: Systematic review approach: 1) Discuss photonic quantum computing architectures, 2) Examine key quantum ML algorithms on photonic platforms (Variational Quantum Circuits, Quantum Neural Networks, Quantum Support Vector Machines), 3) Categorize major noise mechanisms and analyze their impact, 4) Review traditional and advanced noise characterization techniques, 5) Survey recent noise mitigation strategies, 6) Highlight experimental advances and future research directions.
AI.result: The review provides comprehensive analysis of noise sources in PQML systems, including their impact on learning performance, training stability, and convergence behavior. It synthesizes current understanding of noise characterization and mitigation techniques specific to photonic quantum platforms.
AI.conclusion: Noise remains a critical challenge for PQML scalability and reliability. The review identifies key research directions for developing robust PQML systems under realistic noise conditions, emphasizing the need for advanced noise characterization and mitigation strategies to enable practical photonic quantum machine learning implementations.

title: Narrowband heralded single photons via Bragg grating inscription in germanium-doped photonic crystal fiber
summary: We present a fiber-based source of narrowband heralded single photons in the telecoms C-band. Photon pairs were generated by spontaneous four-wave mixing in photonic crystal fiber (PCF) with a germanium-doped region incorporated into its core for enhanced photosensitivity. A fiber Bragg grating (FBG) with a bandwidth of 0.2 nm and contrast of 17.5 dB was UV-written into the PCF to reflect a sub-nanometre slice of the photon-pair spectrum. This allowed narrowband photons to be heralded at the proximal end of the fiber by detection events after the distal end. We present photon counting data with a coincidence-to-accidental ratio of up to 70. Our source demonstrates a viable route to fiber-integrated narrowband heralded single photon sources suitable for coupling to quantum memories and interfacing heterogeneous qubit types.

AI.tldr: Fiber-based narrowband heralded single photon source in telecom C-band using photonic crystal fiber with integrated fiber Bragg grating for spectral filtering.
AI.motivation: Develop fiber-integrated narrowband heralded single photon sources suitable for quantum applications like coupling to quantum memories and interfacing heterogeneous qubit types.
AI.method: Used photonic crystal fiber with germanium-doped core for enhanced photosensitivity, generated photon pairs via spontaneous four-wave mixing, and integrated UV-written fiber Bragg grating (0.2 nm bandwidth, 17.5 dB contrast) for spectral filtering.
AI.result: Achieved coincidence-to-accidental ratio up to 70, demonstrating viable narrowband heralded single photon generation with fiber-integrated approach.
AI.conclusion: The source provides a practical route to fiber-integrated narrowband heralded single photon sources compatible with quantum memory applications and heterogeneous qubit interfaces.

title: Temporal limitations and digital data processing in continuous variable measurements of non-Gaussian states
summary: Non-Gaussian quantum states and operations are essential tools for multiple quantum information protocols exploiting light as information career. In this context, a key role is played by schemes operating with continuous wave light, in which non-Gaussian states are obtained by photon subtraction/addition and eventually reconstructed by quantum state tomography. In these configurations, the temporal resolution of the homodyne detection and the digital data processing critically affect our ability to faithfully reconstruct the produced non-Gaussian states. In this work, we apply digital data processing to experimental data to study how the temporal performances of the detection chain affect the acquisition and treatment of tomographic data. This allows understanding how these features impact the quality of quantum states observed by non-ideal detection chains. By doing so, we discuss the actual constraints on the acquisition and reconstruction of non-Gaussian states by taking into account the limitations of realistic experimental resources.

AI.tldr: Study of how temporal resolution and digital processing affect reconstruction of non-Gaussian quantum states from continuous-wave homodyne tomography data.
AI.motivation: Non-Gaussian quantum states are crucial for quantum information protocols, but their faithful reconstruction via tomography is critically affected by the temporal resolution of homodyne detection and digital data processing in continuous-wave configurations.
AI.method: Applied digital data processing to experimental data to study how temporal performance of detection chain affects acquisition and treatment of tomographic data for non-Gaussian states obtained by photon subtraction/addition.
AI.result: Analysis reveals how detection chain features impact observed quantum state quality, providing understanding of actual constraints on acquisition and reconstruction of non-Gaussian states with realistic experimental resources.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes practical limitations for non-Gaussian state tomography in continuous-wave configurations, highlighting the critical role of temporal resolution and digital processing in achieving faithful quantum state reconstruction.

title: Decoherence-free Behaviors of Quantum Emitters in Dissipative Photonic Graphene
comment: 42 pages, 18 figures. Comments and suggestions are welcome
summary: Achieving decoherence-free quantum state manipulation is a paramount goal in modern quantum technologies. To this end, we demonstrate its implementation in a two-dimensional dissipative photonic graphene featuring exceptional rings. Employing the resolvent method, we analytically explore the quantum dynamics of emitters coupled to photonic graphene. In the thermodynamic limit, our analysis predicts a dissipation-dependent logarithmic relaxation for a single quantum emitter, alongside a pronounced quantum Zeno effect that slows the decay with increased dissipation. Notably, within a finite lattice, the excitation of single quantum emitter stabilizes in a decoherence-protected quantum state, which is identified as a dissipation-robust quasilocalized state. Interestingly, this state, together with a dark state, facilitates decoherence-free interactions between quantum emitters. This capability can be extended to topological graphenic platforms, where edge states mediate analogous protected interactions among giant atoms. Our findings highlight a promising path toward protecting quantum coherence in practical, high-dimensional photonic environment through dissipation engineering.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of decoherence-free quantum state manipulation in 2D dissipative photonic graphene with exceptional rings, enabling dissipation-robust quasilocalized states and protected quantum emitter interactions.
AI.motivation: Achieving decoherence-free quantum state manipulation is crucial for practical quantum technologies, requiring protection of quantum coherence in realistic photonic environments.
AI.method: Employed resolvent method to analytically explore quantum dynamics of emitters coupled to photonic graphene with exceptional rings in thermodynamic and finite lattice limits.
AI.result: Predicted dissipation-dependent logarithmic relaxation for single quantum emitter with quantum Zeno effect; identified dissipation-robust quasilocalized states in finite lattices that enable decoherence-free interactions between quantum emitters; extended capability to topological graphenic platforms with edge states.
AI.conclusion: Dissipation engineering in high-dimensional photonic environments provides a promising path toward protecting quantum coherence for practical quantum technologies.

title: Operational bounds and diagnostics for coherence in energy transfer
summary: Excitation energy transfer in light-harvesting aggregates is highly efficient, yet whether quantum coherence plays an operational role in transport remains debated. A central challenge is that coherence is usually inferred from spectroscopic signatures, whereas transport performance is assessed through specific observables and depends on both the open system dynamics and the initial state preparation. Here we develop a resource theoretic approach that quantifies the maximum change that initial site-basis coherence can induce in a chosen readout under fixed reduced dynamics. The central quantity is the resource impact functional, which yields state independent, readout specific bounds on coherence-induced changes in signals and transport figures of merit. We apply the framework to two models. For a donor-acceptor dimer, we analyse coherence sensitivity across coupling and bath-timescale regimes and bound trapping efficiency and average transfer time in terms of the impact functional. For a multi-site chain with terminal trapping, we derive rigorous criteria that distinguish population placement from sensitivity to initial state site-basis coherence. These include upper bounds on the largest advantage over incoherent preparations, necessary delocalization requirements for achieving a prescribed improvement, and a simple pairwise sufficient condition that can be checked from local information. For quasi-local reduced dynamics, we further obtain a Lieb-Robinson-type bound that constrains when coherence prepared in a distant region can influence a localized readout at finite times. Together, these results provide operational diagnostics and rigorous bounds for benchmarking coherence effects and for identifying regimes in which they are necessarily negligible or potentially relevant in excitonic transport models.

AI.tldr: A resource theory framework quantifies how initial quantum coherence affects transport observables in light-harvesting systems, providing state-independent bounds and diagnostics to assess when coherence matters operationally.
AI.motivation: While quantum coherence is observed in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, its operational role in enhancing transport efficiency remains debated. Current approaches often conflate spectroscopic signatures of coherence with actual transport performance, creating a need for rigorous methods to quantify coherence's functional impact on specific transport observables.
AI.method: Develops a resource theoretic approach with a "resource impact functional" that quantifies the maximum change initial site-basis coherence can induce in chosen readouts under fixed reduced dynamics. The framework provides state-independent, readout-specific bounds on coherence-induced signal changes. Applied to two models: donor-acceptor dimer (analyzing coherence sensitivity across coupling/bath regimes) and multi-site chain with terminal trapping (deriving criteria distinguishing population placement from coherence sensitivity).
AI.result: For dimer: bounds trapping efficiency and average transfer time via impact functional. For chain: derives rigorous criteria including upper bounds on coherence advantage, necessary delocalization requirements, and simple pairwise sufficient condition checkable from local information. For quasi-local dynamics: obtains Lieb-Robinson-type bound constraining when distant coherence can influence localized readouts at finite times.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides operational diagnostics and rigorous bounds for benchmarking coherence effects in excitonic transport, identifying regimes where coherence is necessarily negligible or potentially relevant, thus advancing beyond spectroscopic signatures to functional assessments of quantum effects in biological energy transfer.

title: An Introduction to the Foundations and Interpretations of Quantum Mechanics
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures. Invited submission to Lectures from the 33rd Chris Engelbrecht Summer School, Stellenbosch 2025
summary: This article surveys key conceptual and interpretational developments in quantum mechanics, tracing the theory from its foundational postulates to contemporary discussions of measurement, nonlocality, and the emergence of classicality. Beginning with the structure of Hilbert space and the postulates governing state evolution and measurement, the epistemic stance of the Copenhagen interpretation and its modern reformulations are examined. The Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen argument, Bell's theorem, and Hardy's paradox are then discussed as probes of locality and realism, alongside the deterministic but explicitly nonlocal de Broglie-Bohm theory. The measurement problem and the implications of contextuality are analyzed in relation to objective collapse models, which introduce new physical dynamics to account for definite outcomes. Finally, the role of decoherence in the suppression of interference and the emergence of classical behavior is explored, together with the interpretational frameworks of many-worlds and consistent histories. This material aims to provide a coherent introductory overview of how different interpretations address the central concern of what quantum mechanics tells us about the nature of physical reality.

AI.tldr: A survey paper examining key conceptual developments in quantum mechanics from foundational postulates to modern interpretations, covering measurement, nonlocality, and the emergence of classicality.
AI.motivation: To provide a coherent introductory overview of how different interpretations address the central concern of what quantum mechanics tells us about the nature of physical reality, tracing the theory from its foundational postulates to contemporary discussions.
AI.method: Survey methodology examining: 1) Hilbert space structure and quantum postulates, 2) Copenhagen interpretation and modern reformulations, 3) EPR argument, Bell's theorem, and Hardy's paradox as probes of locality/realism, 4) de Broglie-Bohm theory, 5) measurement problem and contextuality, 6) objective collapse models, 7) decoherence and emergence of classical behavior, 8) many-worlds and consistent histories interpretations.
AI.result: The survey provides a comprehensive overview of quantum mechanics' conceptual landscape, showing how different interpretations address fundamental issues like measurement, nonlocality, and the quantum-to-classical transition, while highlighting ongoing debates about the nature of physical reality.
AI.conclusion: Quantum mechanics presents multiple interpretational frameworks that address the theory's foundational questions differently, with no consensus on which provides the "correct" understanding of physical reality, though all must account for the same empirical predictions.

title: Quantum-preserving telecom conversion of atomic biphotons
comment: Main text: 6 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental material: 2 pages
summary: We experimentally demonstrate telecom frequency conversion of atomic biphotons using a diamond-type atomic ensemble. By spectrally engineering heralded photons and optimizing the atomic converter, efficient conversion is achieved while preserving the temporal waveform and nonclassical antibunching behavior. The converted photons retain strong quantum correlations and well-defined wavepackets, demonstrating preservation of dynamical quantum properties beyond photon-statistics-based benchmarks. The measured performance agrees with a microscopic model that captures the spectral acceptance and parameter dependence of the converter. These results establish a practical interface between atomic photon sources and telecom fiber networks, enabling quantum interference and distributed quantum communication.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of telecom frequency conversion for atomic biphotons using a diamond-type atomic ensemble, preserving quantum properties and enabling fiber network integration.
AI.motivation: To create a practical interface between atomic photon sources and telecom fiber networks for quantum interference and distributed quantum communication applications.
AI.method: Using a diamond-type atomic ensemble as a frequency converter, with spectral engineering of heralded photons and optimization of the atomic converter parameters.
AI.result: Efficient conversion achieved while preserving temporal waveform and nonclassical antibunching behavior; converted photons retain strong quantum correlations and well-defined wavepackets; measured performance matches microscopic model predictions.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a practical quantum interface enabling integration of atomic photon sources with telecom fiber networks for quantum communication applications.

title: Velocity Verlet-based optimization for variational quantum eigensolvers
summary: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is a key algorithm for near-term quantum computers, yet its performance is often limited by the classical optimization of circuit parameters. We propose using the velocity Verlet algorithm, inspired by classical molecular dynamics, to address this challenge. By introducing an inertial "velocity" term, our method efficiently explores complex energy landscapes. We compare its performance against standard optimizers on H$_2$ and LiH molecules. For H$_2$, our method achieves chemical accuracy with fewer quantum circuit evaluations than L-BFGS-B. For LiH, it attains the lowest final energy, demonstrating its potential for high-accuracy VQE simulations.

AI.tldr: Velocity Verlet algorithm applied to VQE optimization reduces quantum circuit evaluations and achieves better accuracy than standard optimizers for molecular systems.
AI.motivation: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is crucial for near-term quantum computing but suffers from inefficient classical optimization of circuit parameters, limiting its practical performance.
AI.method: Proposes using the velocity Verlet algorithm from classical molecular dynamics, which introduces an inertial "velocity" term to efficiently explore complex energy landscapes in VQE parameter optimization.
AI.result: For H₂ molecule, achieves chemical accuracy with fewer quantum circuit evaluations than L-BFGS-B. For LiH, attains the lowest final energy among compared methods.
AI.conclusion: The velocity Verlet algorithm demonstrates superior performance for VQE optimization, offering potential for high-accuracy quantum simulations with reduced computational cost.

title: Crosstalk in Multi-Qubit Fluxonium Architectures with Transmon Couplers
summary: In recent years, several architectures have been proposed for implementing two-qubit operations on fluxonium superconducting qubits. A particularly promising approach, which was demonstrated experimentally by Refs. [1,2], employs a transmon superconducting qubit as a tunable coupler between the fluxonium qubits. These experiments have shown that the transmon coupler enables fast, high-fidelity two-qubit operations while suppressing unwanted ZZ crosstalk between the fluxonium qubits. In this work, we numerically study the scalability of this architecture. We find that, when trivially scaling this architecture, crosstalk from spectator qubits limits the gate fidelity to below 90%. We show that these spectator errors can be reduced to below $10^{-4}$ by reducing the coupling strength and by dynamically tuning transmons that are not used for a two-qubit operation to an off position. We further investigate the resilience of the operation to direct capacitive coupling between the transmon couplers and to microwave crosstalk.

AI.tldr: Numerical study shows that scaling fluxonium-transmon coupler architecture faces spectator qubit crosstalk issues, but can be mitigated by reduced coupling and dynamic tuning of idle transmons.
AI.motivation: To investigate the scalability of the promising fluxonium-transmon coupler architecture for two-qubit operations, which has shown experimental success but may face limitations when scaling to larger systems.
AI.method: Numerical study of the fluxonium-transmon coupler architecture, analyzing crosstalk from spectator qubits, investigating mitigation strategies including reduced coupling strength and dynamic tuning of idle transmons, and examining resilience to direct capacitive coupling and microwave crosstalk.
AI.result: Trivial scaling limits gate fidelity below 90% due to spectator qubit crosstalk, but errors can be reduced below 10^-4 by reducing coupling strength and dynamically tuning unused transmons to off position.
AI.conclusion: The fluxonium-transmon coupler architecture can be scaled effectively with proper mitigation strategies for spectator errors, maintaining high-fidelity two-qubit operations in larger quantum systems.

title: Optimal Universal Bounds for Quantum Divergences
comment: 51 pages, no figures, comments are welcome!
summary: We identify a universal structural principle underlying the smoothing of classical divergences: the optimizer of the smoothing problem is a clipped probability vector, independently of the specific divergence. This yields a divergence-independent characterization of all smoothed classical divergences and reveals a common geometric structure behind seemingly different quantities. Building on this structural insight, we derive optimal universal bounds for smoothed quantum divergences, including quantum R'enyi divergences of arbitrary order and the hypothesis testing divergence. Our inequalities relate divergences of different orders through bounds of the form $D_β^{\varepsilon} \le D_α+ \mathrm{correction}$ and $D_β^{\varepsilon} \ge D_α+ \mathrm{correction}$, and we prove that the correction terms are optimal among all universal, state-independent inequalities of this type. Consequently, our results strictly improve previously known bounds whenever those were suboptimal, and in cases where earlier bounds coincide with ours, our analysis establishes their optimality. In particular, we obtain optimal universal bounds for the hypothesis testing divergence.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a universal structural principle for smoothing classical divergences, showing the optimizer is always a clipped probability vector. This insight enables derivation of optimal universal bounds for smoothed quantum divergences, improving previous results.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental structure underlying smoothed divergences and establish optimal universal bounds for quantum divergences that improve upon existing suboptimal results.
AI.method: Identifies a universal structural principle showing the optimizer of smoothing problems is a clipped probability vector, independent of specific divergence. Uses this insight to derive optimal universal bounds for smoothed quantum divergences including quantum Rényi divergences and hypothesis testing divergence.
AI.result: Derives optimal universal bounds of the form D_β^ε ≤ D_α + correction and D_β^ε ≥ D_α + correction, proving correction terms are optimal among all universal, state-independent inequalities. Results strictly improve previously known bounds when suboptimal and establish optimality when coinciding with earlier bounds.
AI.conclusion: The universal structural principle of clipped probability vectors provides a common geometric foundation for smoothed divergences, enabling derivation of optimal universal bounds that improve and complete the theory of smoothed quantum divergences.

title: Has quantum advantage been achieved?
comment: This is a copyedited version of the original three-part mini series that was published on the Caltech Quantum Frontiers blog
summary: Quantum computational advantage was claimed for the first time in 2019 and several experiments since then have reinforced the claim. And yet, there is no consensus whether or not quantum advantage has actually been achieved. In this article, I address this question and argue that, in fact, it has. I also outline next steps for theory and experiments in quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that quantum computational advantage has indeed been achieved since 2019, despite ongoing debate, and outlines future directions for theory and experiments.
AI.motivation: To resolve the ongoing debate about whether quantum computational advantage has actually been achieved since it was first claimed in 2019, despite several subsequent experiments supporting the claim.
AI.method: The author presents an argumentative analysis and position statement rather than experimental results, examining the evidence and claims from quantum advantage experiments since 2019.
AI.result: The author concludes that quantum computational advantage has indeed been achieved, providing a definitive position on the ongoing debate.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computational advantage has been achieved, and the paper outlines next steps for both theoretical development and experimental work to advance the field further.

title: Hysteretic squashed entanglement in many-body quantum systems
summary: Entanglement in many-body quantum systems is distributed across spatial regions, where its structure often dictates the information-processing capabilities of the state. Yet, characterizing the entanglement structure, especially for mixed states, remains a challenge. In this work, we propose hysteretic squashed entanglement $T_{sq}$, a conditional entanglement monotone that measures the genuine quantum correlations between two subregions, conditioned on a third region, in a many-body quantum state. $T_{sq}$ is upper bounded by the convex-roof extension of quantum conditional mutual information and exhibits several desirable properties like monogamy, convexity, asymptotic continuity, faithfulness, and additivity for tensor-product states. We study the conditional entanglement generation in a one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model under quench, where we show that $T_{sq}$ effectively squashes classical contributions and can detect genuine quantum correlations across both adjacent and long-range subsystems. We elucidate the utility of this measure as a robust quantifier of topological entanglement entropy for mixed states. This opens new operational resource-theoretic avenues for probing topological order and criticality.

AI.tldr: Proposes hysteretic squashed entanglement (T_sq), a conditional entanglement monotone for many-body quantum systems that measures genuine quantum correlations between two subregions conditioned on a third region, with applications to detecting topological order in mixed states.
AI.motivation: Characterizing entanglement structure in many-body quantum systems, especially for mixed states, remains challenging. Existing measures often fail to distinguish genuine quantum correlations from classical contributions, limiting understanding of information-processing capabilities and topological order.
AI.method: Introduces hysteretic squashed entanglement (T_sq), a conditional entanglement monotone based on convex-roof extension of quantum conditional mutual information. The measure squashes classical correlations and satisfies desirable properties: monogamy, convexity, asymptotic continuity, faithfulness, and additivity for tensor-product states. Applied to study conditional entanglement generation in 1D transverse-field Ising model under quench dynamics.
AI.result: T_sq effectively squashes classical contributions and detects genuine quantum correlations across both adjacent and long-range subsystems. The measure serves as a robust quantifier of topological entanglement entropy for mixed states, enabling detection of topological order in non-pure quantum states.
AI.conclusion: Hysteretic squashed entanglement provides a powerful operational resource-theoretic tool for probing topological order and criticality in many-body quantum systems, particularly for mixed states where traditional entanglement measures are inadequate.

title: Quantum control of the environment in open quantum systems enables rapid qubit reset
summary: Qubit reset is crucial in quantum technology and is typically achieved by coupling the qubit to a dissipative environment. However, the achievable speed and fidelity are limited by qubit-environment entanglement. We use exact tensor-network simulations and a time-dependent variational approach to investigate these effects for transmon qubits with a time-dependent system-environment coupling. We show that they are due to the formation of a polaron state and how this can be reversed using a time-dependent coupling. Coupling protocols are identified which achieve reset with an excited-state population of $10^{-6}$ in $10$ ns. A related paper [C. Ortega-Taberner, E. O'Neill and P. R. Eastham, arXiv:XXXX.XXXX] addresses the complementary case of control via a time-dependent Hamiltonian. Our work shows how the dynamics of the environment of an open quantum system can be controlled to design effective quantum processes in non-Markovian systems.

AI.tldr: Qubit reset via time-dependent system-environment coupling achieves high-fidelity, fast reset by reversing polaron formation through optimized coupling protocols.
AI.motivation: Qubit reset is essential for quantum technology, but conventional methods are limited by qubit-environment entanglement that restricts speed and fidelity. The authors aim to overcome these limitations by controlling the system-environment coupling dynamics.
AI.method: The authors use exact tensor-network simulations and a time-dependent variational approach to study transmon qubits with time-dependent system-environment coupling. They analyze polaron state formation and develop optimized coupling protocols to reverse this effect.
AI.result: The research identifies coupling protocols that achieve qubit reset with excited-state population of 10⁻⁶ in 10 ns. They demonstrate that polaron formation limits conventional reset methods and show how time-dependent coupling can reverse this effect.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates how controlling environment dynamics through time-dependent coupling enables effective quantum processes in non-Markovian systems, achieving high-fidelity, fast qubit reset by reversing polaron formation.

title: Qubit reset beyond the Born-Markov approximation: optimal driving to overcome polaron formation
summary: Qubits are typically reset into a known state by coupling them to a low-temperature environment. When treated in the Born-Markov approximation such couplings produce exponential relaxation to equilibrium, giving high reset fidelities limited only by temperature. We investigate qubit reset beyond this approximation, using numerically exact tensor network methods and the time-dependent variational principle, focussing on a spin-boson model describing a transmon qubit coupled to a resistor. Beyond the Born-Markov approximation the reset fidelity becomes limited by the buildup of system-environment correlations which corresponds to the formation of a polaron. We implement numerical optimal control to find time-dependent qubit Hamiltonians which overcome this limitation by steering the dynamics of the correlated system-environment state. The optimal controls becomes more effective when the environment is filtered to span a smaller spectral range, and remain effective when the multilevel nature of the transmon is considered. A related paper [C. Ortega-Taberner, E. O'Neill and P. R. Eastham, arXiv:XXXX.XXXX] addresses the complementary case of control via a time-dependent system-environment coupling. Our results show how limitations on reset speed and fidelity can be overcome, and how time-dependent driving can steer system-environment correlations and reverse polaron formation.

AI.tldr: Qubit reset beyond Born-Markov approximation shows fidelity limited by system-environment correlations (polaron formation), but optimal control can overcome these limitations by steering correlated dynamics.
AI.motivation: Traditional qubit reset methods using Born-Markov approximation achieve high fidelities limited only by temperature, but beyond this approximation, reset fidelity becomes limited by system-environment correlations (polaron formation). The paper investigates how to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: Uses numerically exact tensor network methods and time-dependent variational principle to study spin-boson model of transmon qubit coupled to a resistor. Implements numerical optimal control to find time-dependent qubit Hamiltonians that steer correlated system-environment dynamics.
AI.result: Optimal controls overcome polaron formation limitations, becoming more effective when environment is filtered to smaller spectral range. Controls remain effective when considering transmon's multilevel nature. Shows limitations on reset speed and fidelity can be overcome.
AI.conclusion: Time-dependent driving can steer system-environment correlations and reverse polaron formation, demonstrating how to overcome fundamental limitations on qubit reset speed and fidelity beyond Born-Markov approximations.
